Siopa Mobile, Release Notes Siopa is the shopping app for SuperValu Gaeltacht stores, built by a team of six at Údarás na Gaeltachta's innovation hub in Gaoth Dobhair. This changelog lists each version and explains changes that users or store staff asked about. Version 2.6.0, 28 September 2026 1. Customers can now choose a one-hour collection slot instead of a three-hour window. 2. Substitution preferences can be set per item, including "no substitute". 3. The app is now fully available in Irish and English, switchable from the profile screen at any time. 4. Store staff see a new picking screen that groups items by aisle.
5. Fixed a crash on Android 15 when scanning loyalty cards with the camera.

Narrower 

collection slots were the most requested feature in our summer survey, particularly from customers in Carraroe and Dingle who combine shopping trips with school pickups. Stores now limit each slot to six orders, so slots

 may fill up more quickly at busy times.

Per-item substitution preferences address a long-standing frustration. Previously, customers could only accept or refuse all substitutions, which led to unwanted swaps for items such as baby formula, where brand matters. Each item in the basket now
has a small toggle beside it. Irish-language support existed in earlier versions but was incomplete, with checkout and account screens appearing only in English. Translation was completed with help from the Gaeloideachas volunteers who reviewed every screen.

The aisle-grouped picking screen came from the staff at the Rath Chairn store, who pointed out that the old list followed the order customers added items, sending pickers back and forth across the shop. Average picking time for a 40-item order has 
fallen from 22 minutes to 15 in testing. Version 2.5.2, 9 August 2026 1. Corrected the display of multi-buy offers that showed the wrong total price. 2. Improved app start-up time on older iPhones.

The multi-buy bug charged customers correctly at checkout but displayed a higher total in the basket, which understandably caused alarm. No customer was overcharged, and we apologise for the confusion. Version 2.5.0, 1 July 2026 1. Added the ability to reorder a previous basket with a single tap. 2. Introduced push notifications for order status.

Reordering previous baskets saves time for customers with regular weekly shops. Notifications are optional and can be turned off in settings. Known Issues On some Samsung devices, the Irish keyboard autocorrects product search terms into English words. We are investigating with Samsung. In the meantime, turning off predictive text for search resolves the issue.

Feedback Please send comments or problems to siopa@udaras.ie, or speak to staff in your local store. Our product lead, Caitríona Ní Ghallchóir, reads every message.

Ibn Sina (; 980 – June 1037 CE), commonly known in the West as Avicenna (), was the preeminent philosopher and physician of the Muslim world, flourishing during the Islamic Golden Age, serving in the courts of various Iranian rulers. He is often described as the father of early modern medicine. His philosophy was of the Muslim Peripatetic school derived from Aristotelianism.

His most famous works are The Book of Healing, a philosophical and scientific encyclopedia, and The Canon of Medicine, a medical encyclopedia which became a standard medical text at many medieval universities and remained in use as late as 1650. Besides philosophy and medicine, Avicenna's corpus includes writings on astronomy, alchemy, geography and geology, psychology, Islamic theology, logic, mathematics, physics, and works of poetry.

Avicenna wrote most of his philosophical and scientific works in Arabic, but also wrote several key works in Persian, while his poetic works were written in both languages. Of the 450 works he is believed to have written, around 240 have survived, including 150 on philosophy and 40 on medicine.

Name
is a Latin corruption of the Arabic patronym Ibn Sīnā (), meaning "Son of Sina". However, Avicenna was not the son but the great-great-grandson of a man named Sina. His formal Arabic name was Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥusayn bin ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Ḥasan bin ʿAlī bin Sīnā al-Balkhi al-Bukhari ().

Circumstances
Avicenna created an extensive corpus of works during what is commonly known as the Islamic Golden Age, in which the translations of Byzantine Greco-Roman, Persian and Indian texts were studied extensively. Greco-Roman (Mid- and Neo-Platonic, and Aristotelian) texts translated by the Kindi school were commented, redacted and developed substantially by Islamic intellectuals, who also built upon Persian and Indian mathematical systems, astronomy, algebra, trigonometry and medicine.

The Samanid dynasty in the eastern part of Persia, Greater Khorasan and Central Asia as well as the Buyid dynasty in the western part of Persia and Iraq provided a thriving atmosphere for scholarly and cultural development. Under the Samanids, Bukhara rivaled Baghdad as a cultural capital of the Islamic world. There, Avicenna had access to the great libraries of Balkh, Khwarezm, Gorgan, Rey, Isfahan and Hamadan.

Various texts (such as the 'Ahd with Bahmanyar) show that Avicenna debated philosophical points with the greatest scholars of the time. Aruzi Samarqandi describes how before Avicenna left Khwarezm he had met Al-Biruni (a famous scientist and astronomer), Abu Nasr Iraqi (a renowned mathematician), Abu Sahl Masihi (a respected philosopher) and Abu al-Khayr Khammar (a great physician). The study of the Quran and the Hadith also thrived, and Islamic philosophy, fiqh and theology (kalaam) were all further developed by Avicenna and his opponents at this time.

Biography

Early life and education
Avicenna was born in in the village of Afshana in Transoxiana to a family of Persian stock. The village was near the Samanid capital of Bukhara, which was his mother's hometown. His father Abd Allah was a native of the city of Balkh in Tukharistan. An official of the Samanid bureaucracy, he had served as the governor of a village of the royal estate of Harmaytan (near Bukhara) during the reign of Nuh II (). Avicenna also had a younger brother. A few years later, the family settled in Bukhara, a center of learning, which attracted many scholars. It was there that Avicenna was educated, which early on was seemingly administered by his father. Although both Avicenna's father and brother had converted to Ismailism, he himself did not follow the faith. He was instead an adherent of the Sunni Hanafi school, which was also followed by the Samanids.

Marathi Language Day is either of the two popular days being celebrated in the Indian state of Maharashtra where Marathi language is primarily spoken.
1st May - "Marathi Official Language Day" (मराठी राजभाषा दिन)
27th February - "Marathi Language Pride Day" (मराठी भाषा गौरव दिन)

1 May
On 1 May 1960, the erstwhile Bombay State was divided into the current states of Maharashtra and Gujarat based on primary spoken languages as Marathi and Gujarati. The day is hence also celebrated in Maharashtra as Maharashtra Day (महाराष्ट्र दिन) and is observed as state holiday. Marathi thus became the "Official Language" of the state from 1 May 1960. The Government of Maharashtra issued notice on 5 July 1960 establishing Directorate of Languages. As per "Maharashtra Official Language Act 1964", Marathi language officially received the status of Official Language. From 1 May 1966, the Marathi Official Language Act was implemented in all government affairs in the state. Book title Introduction to Raj Bhasha was also published for non-Marathi speaking government officials. However, in due course of time, due to the fanfare celebrations of Maharashtra Day and Labour Day; both being observed on 1 May, the Marathi Official Language Day celebrations had reduced and also being ignored by government bodies. On 10 April 1977, the government issued another circular about reminder of this day and its observances. In the revived events, various functions and competitions were encouraged to be arranged on local levels from 28 April to 30 April with conclusion ceremonies held on 1 May.

27 February
Vishnu Vaman Shirwadkar, popularly known by his pen name, Kusumagraj, was a celebrated Marathi author who was honoured with Jnanpith Award in 1987. He made significant contribution in the cultural field of Maharashtra and tireless efforts to make Marathi the language of knowledge. On 21 January 2023, Maharashtra Government issued circular to celebrate 27 February, birthday of Kusumagraj, as "Marathi Language Pride Day".

Celebrations
Essay competitions and seminars are arranged in Schools and Colleges. Government officials are asked to conduct various events.

Construction Management, Module 6: Planning a Kitchen Renovation as a Small Project

Notes from the lecture by Ing. Erik Verhulst, Hogeschool PXL, Hasselt. These notes summarise the main content of the session and the example used in class. They do not replace the slides or the reading on the course platform.

Why a Kitchen? Most of you will start your careers managing renovation projects for homeowners or small contractors rather than large building sites. A kitchen renovation is an ideal training case, because it 
involves several trades working in a small space, a client who lives in the house during the works, and a sequence of tasks where a single delay ripples through everything that follows. Erik used the example of a semi-detached house in Genk renovated by his former company in 2024, with a budget of 28,000 euros and a planned duration of five weeks.

The Sequence of Trades

The core of the lecture was the logical order of activities. Erik insisted that most problems on small projects come from getting this order wrong. In the Genk example, the sequence was planned as follows: * Removal of the old kitchen and disconnection of water, gas and electricity * Demolition and any structural work, such as widening an opening * First fix of plumbing and electrical work, while walls and floors are still open * Plastering of walls and screeding of floors, followed by drying time * Floor tiling and wall finishes * Installation of kitchen units, then measurement of the worktop
* Worktop installation, followed by second fix of plumbing and electrics Drying time is often underestimated. A cement screed of five centimetres needs at least three to four weeks before tiles can be laid, unless a fast-drying product is used. In the Genk case the planner had allowed only one week, which delayed the whole project by two weeks and forced the clients to cook in their garage for longer than they had been promised. Communication With the Client A large part
of the session dealt with the client relationship. Erik advised us to agree on a clear decision deadline for every choice the client must make, such as tiles, handles and appliances, and to write these deadlines into the planning. In his experience, late client decisions cause more delays than any technical issue. He also recommended a short weekly update by email, even when nothing special has happened, because clients living in a building site become anxious when they hear nothing.

Cost Control We briefly discussed contingency. For renovations in older Flemish homes, Erik recommends a contingency of at least ten percent, because hidden problems such as damp walls or outdated wiring are common. Exercise

For the workshop next week, prepare a bar chart planning for a kitchen renovation of your choice, including drying times and client decision deadlines. Work in pairs and bring a printed version.

Moving a Reservations Database from MySQL 5.7 to PostgreSQL 16

At Hostales del Caribe, our booking system for eleven guesthouses in Cartagena and Santa Marta ran on MySQL 5.7 for almost a decade. When the version reached end of support, we decided to move to PostgreSQL rather than upgrade in place, mainly for better JSON handling and stricter data validation. This tutorial describes the approach our team used, so you can adapt it to a small or medium database of your own. Our database held about 14 gigabytes across 63 tables.

Before You Start

Take an inventory of everything that touches the database: the web application, the nightly accounting export, reporting dashboards and any scripts people have written over the years. We found four forgotten cron jobs on an old server in the Santa Marta office that wrote directly to the bookings table. Write down each one, because every connection string will need to change.

The Migration Steps

We used pgloader, an open-source tool that reads a MySQL database and creates the equivalent schema and data in PostgreSQL. The steps we followed were:

1. Create an empty PostgreSQL 16 database and a user with the same privileges the application needs.
2. Run pgloader against a copy of production restored on a test server, never against production itself.
3. Review the generated schema and fix type mappings, especially tinyint columns that MySQL used as booleans.
4. Replace MySQL-specific SQL in the application, such as backtick quoting, IFNULL and GROUP_CONCAT.
5. Run the full application test suite against the new database and compare row counts table by table.
6. Schedule a maintenance window, set the old database to read-only, run pgloader one final time and switch the connection strings.

Problems We Hit

Dates caused the most trouble. MySQL had allowed zero dates such as 0000-00-00 in the check-out column, which PostgreSQL rejects. Pgloader converts them to null by default, but our application treated null as an open-ended stay, so we had to correct about 300 old records by hand before migrating. Text comparisons also behaved differently, because MySQL's default collation is case-insensitive while PostgreSQL's is not; guest searches by surname stopped finding matches until we added the citext extension to the relevant columns.

After the Switch

Keep the old MySQL server running in read-only mode for at least a month in case you need to check something. Our maintenance window, from 01:00 to 04:30 on a Tuesday in February, finished with forty minutes to spare. Developer Luisa Fernanda Pérez wrote the comparison scripts we used, and they are available on our internal repository for anyone attempting a similar move.

input: The 68th Oregon Legislative Assembly was the legislative session of the Oregon Legislative Assembly that convened on January 9, 1995, and adjourned June 10 the same year. Senate Bill Bradbury resigned April 16, 1995, and Brenda Brecke replaced him the next day. They were both Democrats. Wes Cooley resigned January 3, 1995, and Greg Walden was sworn in 6 days later on January 9. They were both Republicans. Marylin Shannon was sworn on January 11, 1995, in replacement of Jim Bunn, who resigned January 3, 1995. They were both Republicans. Senate Members House Ray Baum resigned as Majority Leader on August 4, 1995. Lynn Lundquist was appointed Majority Leader on August 4, 1995, to fill the vacancy. Timothy Josi resigned on October 1, 1995, and was then reappointed on October 3, 1995. Tony Federici passed away while in office on August 30, 1995. Jackie Taylor was appointed on October 5, 1995, to fill the vacancy. House Members

Curriculum Studies 312, Lecture 5: 
Introducing Information Studies as a Compulsory
 Subject Lecturer: Associate Professor Wataru Seno. Notes typed up by student volunteer Hinako Asai, 30 September 2026. Corrections welcome on the course forum.

T
oday's lecture
 used the introduction of Information I as a compulsory upper secondary subject in Japan, which became part of the national curriculum from April 2022, as a case study in how a major curriculum change reaches classrooms. The subject covers programming, data handling, networks and information ethics, and from the 2025 university entrance tests it also appears in the common test taken by most applicants. The Policy Logic Professor Seno described the change as a response to two pressures. First, employers and government reports had warned for years of a shortage of people with digital skills. Second, the earlier optional subjects in information studies were taught very unevenly, with many schools treating them as typing practice or office software training. Making the subject compulsory and placing it in the common test was meant to force schools to take it seriously. Implementation Challenges * Teacher supply: many prefectures had too few teachers licensed in information studies and relied on temporary licences * Equipment: schools varied widely in the number and quality of computers available * Textbooks: publishers had little time to develop materials before the first cohort began
* Assessment: teachers were unsure how to grade programming work fairly and consistently Evidence From the First Years

We looked at a 2024 survey by a prefectural education centre in Tochigi, which found that about a third of teachers delivering the subject held only a temporary licence. Teachers with a permanent licence reported much more confiden
ce in teaching programming than those without. Students' views were mixed: many said they enjoyed programming tasks, but a significant minority found the pace too fast and felt the subjec
t was being taught mainly as preparation for the entrance test. Discussion Questions for Next Week * Is linking a new subject to high-stakes testing a good way to ensure it is taught properly? * What could prefectures have done earlier to prepare enough qualified teachers? * How should teachers balance exam preparation with broader digital literacy? Please read the two articles posted on the course site before the seminar, including the chapter by Professor Mitsuko Taira on curriculum reform in the 1990s, which offers a useful comparison with the earlier introduction of integrated studies.

Curriculum Studies 312, Lecture 5: Introducing Information Studies as a Compulsory Subject

Lecturer: Associate Professor Wataru Seno. Notes typed up by student volunteer Hinako Asai, 30 September 2026. Corrections welcome on the course forum.

Today's lecture used the introduction of Information I as a compulsory upper secondary subject in Japan, which became part of the national curriculum from April 2022, as a case study in how a major curriculum change reaches classrooms. The subject covers programming, data handling, networks and information ethics, and from the 2025 university entrance tests it also appears in the common test taken by most applicants.

The Policy Logic

Professor Seno described the change as a response to two pressures. First, employers and government reports had warned for years of a shortage of people with digital skills. Second, the earlier optional subjects in information studies were taught very unevenly, with many schools treating them as typing practice or office software training. Making the subject compulsory and placing it in the common test was meant to force schools to take it seriously.

Implementation Challenges

* Teacher supply: many prefectures had too few teachers licensed in information studies and relied on temporary licences
* Equipment: schools varied widely in the number and quality of computers available
* Textbooks: publishers had little time to develop materials before the first cohort began
* Assessment: teachers were unsure how to grade programming work fairly and consistently

Evidence From the First Years

We looked at a 2024 survey by a prefectural education centre in Tochigi, which found that about a third of teachers delivering the subject held only a temporary licence. Teachers with a permanent licence reported much more confidence in teaching programming than those without. Students' views were mixed: many said they enjoyed programming tasks, but a significant minority found the pace too fast and felt the subject was being taught mainly as preparation for the entrance test.

Discussion Questions for Next Week

* Is linking a new subject to high-stakes testing a good way to ensure it is taught properly?
* What could prefectures have done earlier to prepare enough qualified teachers?
* How should teachers balance exam preparation with broader digital literacy?

Please read the two articles posted on the course site before the seminar, including the chapter by Professor Mitsuko Taira on curriculum reform in the 1990s, which offers a useful comparison with the earlier introduction of integrated studies.

Case Summary: Ventos do Sertão Energia S.A. v. Turbomar Serviços Técnicos Ltda. Court: 3rd Business Court of the District of Natal, Rio Grande do Norte. Judgment of 4 August 2026. Appeal pending before the State Court of Justice.

Nature of the Dispute

The claimant operates a 96-megawatt wind farm near João Câmara comprising forty Siemens Gamesa turbines. In 2022 it entered into a five-year operation and maintenance agreement with the respondent, a specialised service company, under which the respondent undertook preventive maintenance according to the manufacturer's schedule, corrective repairs within defined response times, and a guaranteed availability of 96 percent averaged across each contractual year. In March 2025 the gearbox on turbine WTG-23 failed catastrophically. The claimant alleged that the failure resulted from the respondent's omission of two scheduled oil analyses and claimed R$ 7.4 million in repair costs and lost generation. Questions Considered

The court addressed several connected questions:

- Whether the omitted oil analyses constituted a breach of the maintenance obligations
- Whether that breach caused the gearbox failure, given expert evidence of a possible manufacturing defect - Whether the contractual limitation of liability, capped at the annual contract price, applied
- Whether lost generation was recoverable or excluded as indirect loss

Findings on Breach and Causation The court found that the respondent's own service records showed that oil samples for WTG-23 were not taken in the third and fourth quarters of 2024, in breach of the maintenance plan incorporated into the contract. On causation, the court-appointed expert, Engineer Lúcia Medeiros, concluded that metal particle levels would very probably have revealed bearing wear at least four months before failure, allowing a planned bearing replacement at a fraction of the cost. The respondent's argument that a casting defect in the planet carrier caused the failure was rejected, as metallurgical analysis showed fatigue cracking originating at the worn bearing.

Limitation of Liability The contract capped the respondent's liability at the annual service fee, which was R$ 3.1 million in 2025. The claimant argued that the cap should not apply because the omission amounted to gross negligence. The court disagreed, finding that while the omission was serious, it resulted from a scheduling error during a change of site supervisors rather than deliberate disregard of obligations. The cap was therefore upheld. Lost Generation

The contract excluded indirect and consequential losses but did not define them. Applying Article 403 of the Civil Code, the court held that lost revenue from the turbine's downtime was a direct and immediate consequence of the failure and was recoverable, subject to the overall cap.

Outcome

The respondent was ordered to pay R$ 3.1 million, the full amount of the cap, with monetary correction and interest from the date of the claim. Both parties have appealed: the claimant on the application of the cap, and the respondent on causation. Practical Note Operators negotiating maintenance agreements should define indirect loss explicitly and consider whether liability caps should be disapplied for failures to perform core condition monitoring tasks.

Break the Safe is a BBC National Lottery game show which was broadcast on BBC One from 27 July 2013 to 30 August 2014. It was hosted by Nick Knowles.

Format
On each episode, three teams of two contestants apiece answer questions to accumulate prize money, which is placed into a large safe in the studio. The safe is secured with six locks, and a 36-minute countdown clock runs throughout the game. Four of the locks are opened during the course of the show; the last team remaining must open the other two in order to win the money, up to £100,000.

Round 1
The teams stand at podiums that are split down the middle, allowing each contestant to be pushed forward or backward by pneumatics, and the three in the left positions are pushed back to start the round. The host asks 12 questions on the buzzer, each of which has two correct answers. Only the contestants in front may buzz-in; once a contestant does so, they must give one answer and their partner in back must then give the other. If both answers are correct, the team wins £1,000; if not, the host begins re-reading the question and either of the other teams may buzz-in. A second miss results in the question being discarded. Contestants may buzz-in at any time, but must answer based only on whatever information the host has read to that point.

After the 12 questions have been asked, the contestants' positions are reversed and the host asks a second set of 12 questions worth £2,000 each. The round ends after this set, the lowest-scoring team is eliminated with no winnings, and the totals of the remaining two teams are put into the safe. A maximum of £36,000 can be accumulated in this round by the two teams that advance.

Round 2
The scores are reset to zero, and each team chooses one of its members to be pushed back. The host asks one question to each team, starting with the one that brought less money through from Round 1. After hearing a question, the teammate in front may either answer it immediately, or pass it to their partner for double value without being able to see if the partner knows the answer.

Three pairs of questions are played, worth £2,000/£4,000, £4,000/£8,000, and £6,000/£12,000. The team members' positions are reversed for the second pair, while each team again chooses who will move forward or back for the third.

After all six questions have been asked, the team with the lower total is eliminated with no winnings, and the higher-scoring team's money is added to the safe. A team can accumulate up to £24,000 in this round. The Thunderball draw is then held.

Round 3
The team is asked four questions, but each member may only answer two of them. Before each question, the host names a category and the team decides who will answer. Each correct answer allows the team to either add £10,000 to the safe or expand their "window of opportunity" to open it by one second. The team starts with a window of one second; depending on the number of correct answers and extra seconds taken, it can become as long as five seconds. The team can accumulate up to £40,000 in this round by answering every question correctly and taking the money on each.

Round 4
Each teammate is given a button that controls one of the two still-closed locks on the safe, and a partition is placed between them to prevent any communication. When the countdown clock reaches 30 seconds, it disappears from the team's view. Both teammates must continue the countdown in their heads; once they believe it has reached zero, they must push their buttons within the length of their window of opportunity to open the locks. The National Lottery draw is held after both contestants have pushed their buttons.

Following the draw, the results are revealed. If both buttons were pushed within the window, the team wins all the money in the safe. The team wins half the money if one button was pushed in time, or nothing at all if both buttons were pushed too early or too late.

The AquaVit Tatra 1100 is a submersible garden pump for clean and lightly dirty water, designed for rain barrels, cisterns and garden ponds up to seven metres deep. It is manufactured in Prešov by Hydrotech Šariš s.r.o. and sold through garden centres in Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary. Technical Specifications • Rated power: 1,100 W at 230 V and 50 Hz. • Maximum flow: 5,400 litres per hour at zero head. • Maximum delivery head: 38 metres, suitable for sprinklers on two-storey plots. • Maximum particle size: 5 mm, handled by the stainless steel inlet strainer.
• Cable length: 10 metres with a rubber H07RN-F sheath. • Weight: 7.9 kg without hose. Float Switch and Dry Running The pump starts and stops automatically by means of an adjustable float switch fixed to the carrying handle. When the water level falls to about 14 cm above the base, the float drops and the motor stops before air enters the impeller. You can shorten or lengthen the free cable of the float to change the switching range, but never fix the float in the upper position, because the internal thermal cut-out is only a last resort and repeated triggering shortens the life of the seals. Pressure Output Module From the 2026 model year the Tatra 1100 accepts the optional PK-2 pressure module, which screws onto the outlet and keeps a constant pressure of 2.2 bar for drip lines and garden taps. With the module fitted, the pump starts when a tap is opened and stops about eight seconds after it is closed. The module also includes a small expansion chamber that reduces the number of starts per hour, which matters for owners who water by hand with frequent short bursts.

Installation Notes Lower the pump on a rope tied to the handle, never by the power cable. Place it on a flat stone or brick if the bottom of the tank holds sludge, since a layer of sediment can clog the strainer
within a single season. The outlet takes a 1 inch threaded connector, and a reducing adapter for 3/4 inch hose is supplied in the box. Warranty and Service Hydrotech Šariš offers a three-year warranty when the pump is registered on its website within thirty days of pu
rchase. Authorised service points are listed by region, and the nearest one for most customers in eastern Slovakia is the workshop in Sabinov.

Luce Balcone 800 Plug-In Solar Kit, User Manual

Small balcony solar systems have become popular in Italian cities because they can be installed without a roofer and connected through a dedicated outlet. The Luce Balcone 800 consists of
 two 400 W panels, a microinverter and a mounting frame that hooks over a standard balcon
y railing. Please read this manual completely before installation. The kit may only be connected to a circuit checked by an electrician, and you must notify your distribution operator before first use, as explained in section 4. 1 
What You Need Besides the contents of the box, you will need a cordless drill, a spirit level, a 13 mm spanner and a second person to help lift the panels. Each panel weighs 20 kg and measures 1.72 by 1.13 metres, and it can catch the wind like a sail, so never handle it alone on a windy

day. 2 Mounting on the Railing The frame fits railings with a top bar between 30 and 60 mm thick. Follow these steps in order: 1. Attach the two upper hooks to the frame at the height marked for your railing type. 2. Hang the frame on the outside
of the railing and secure the hooks with t
he clamping bolts, tightened to 25 Nm. 3. Fix the lower stabiliser arms against the railing posts so the frame cannot swing. 4. Lift the first panel into the frame and fasten it with the four clamps provided. 5. Repeat for the second panel and check that both sit level. 6. Attach the microinverter to the back of the frame with the bracket supplied. 3 Electrical Connection Connect each panel to the microinverter using the MC4 cables, pressing the connectors until they click. The microinverter output cable ends in a plug that must go into an outdoor socket with an IP44 rating or higher, on a circuit protected by a residual current device. Do not use extension leads or multi-plug adapters. The inverter limits output to 800 W, the maximum allowed for this type of system without additional paperwork. 4 Notifying the Grid O
perator Italian rules require that every generator connected to the network be registered. You can do this on the Terna Gau
dì portal or through the simplified form of your distribution operator, which in most cities is E-Dis
tribuzione, Areti in Rome 
or Unareti in Milan and Brescia. The form asks for the serial number of the microinverter, printed on its label and on the warranty card. Registration is free, and your meter may be replaced with a bidirectional model at no cost. 5 Everyday Use

The system starts automatically each morning and needs no attention. In a south-facing position in central Italy it produces about 900 to 1,000 kWh per year, which covers the daytime consumption of a refrigerator and a router with energy left for other appliances. Clean the panels with water and a soft brush twice a year, and check the clamping bolts after severe storms.

4. Lift the first panel into the frame and fasten it with the four clamps provided.
5. Repeat for the second panel and check that both sit level.
6. Attach the microinverter to the back of the frame with the bracket supplied.

3 Electrical Connection

Connect each panel to the microinverter using the MC4 cables, pressing the connectors until they click. The microinverter output cable ends in a plug that must go into an outdoor socket with an IP44 rating or higher, on a circuit protected by a residual current device. Do not use extension leads or multi-plug adapters. The inverter limits output to 800 W, the maximum allowed for this type of system without additional paperwork.

4 Notifying the Grid Operator

Italian rules require that every generator connected to the network be registered. You can do this on the Terna Gaudì portal or through the simplified form of your distribution operator, which in most cities is E-Distribuzione, Areti in Rome or Unareti in Milan and Brescia. The form asks for the serial number of the microinverter, printed on its label and on the warranty card. Registration is free, and your meter may be replaced with a bidirectional model at no cost.

5 Everyday Use

The system starts automatically each morning and needs no attention. In a south-facing position in central Italy it produces about 900 to 1,000 kWh per year, which covers the daytime consumption of a refrigerator and a router with energy left for other appliances. Clean the panels with water and a soft brush twice a year, and check the clamping bolts after severe storms.

Jack Donnelly (born 28 October 1985) is an English actor, best known for his role in BBC series Atlantis, in which he played the role of Jason. Early life Donnelly was born the first of four boys in Bournemouth on 28 October 1985, the son of Chrissie Wickham and Tony Donnelly. His mother was the choreographer of Bucks Fizz's winning dance routine at the 1981 Eurovision Song Contest, as well as an actress and former Hot Gossip dance troupe member. He was raised primarily in Ringwood, Hampshire. He attended St Catherine's Primary School in Wimborne Minster, Dorset, and then St Peter's School in Bournemouth. He later joined the Big Little Theatre School in Bournemouth.

Career
Donnelly is a founding member of the improvisational comedy group "Chuckle Duster", which performs occasionally in east London. Donnelly's first acting was as Jason Winkler in Nickelodeon's TV series House of Anubis. He then guest starred in shows such as Doctors, Threesome, Misfits, Dancing on the Edge. In 2013, he landed a lead role in BBC's fantasy series Atlantis, where he played the role of Jason who washes up on the shores of the ancient and mysterious city of Atlantis. In 2014, he played the role of a cocky footballer Olly Hunter 
in the wholly improvised spoof documentary United We Fall. In 2016, he guest starred as Samuel Walker in the TV series Death in Paradise.

In 2017, Donnelly played lead role of Prince Adrian in the Hallmark original movie A Royal Winter alongside Merritt Patterson. Personal life In October 2017, Donnelly became engaged to Swedish-Canadian actress Malin Åkerman. They were married in Tulum on 1 December 2018. Filmography Film Television

It is the last psalm in the final Davidic collection of psalms, comprising Psalms 138 to 145, which are specifically attributed to David in their opening verses.

In the slightly different numbering system used in the Greek Septuagint version of the Bible, and in the Latin Vulgate, this psalm is Psalm 144. The psalm is a hymn psalm.

The psalm forms a regular part of Jewish, Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and other Protestant liturgies. It has often been set to music, notably by Antonín Dvořák who set several verses in Czech in his Biblical Songs.

Background and themes
This is the only psalm which identifies itself as a תְּהִלָה (tehillah) – as a psalm (namely, a hymn of praise). The version in the Dead Sea Scrolls instead describes itself as a "prayer" although it does not contain any request.

Psalm 145 is an alphabetic acrostic, the initial letter of each verse being the Hebrew alphabet in sequence. For this purpose, the usual Hebrew numbering of verse 1, which begins with the title, "A Psalm of David", is ignored in favor of the non-Hebrew numbering which treats verse 1 as beginning ארוממך (Aromimkha, "I will exalt You").

The Dead Sea Scrolls version also ends each verse with the recurring (non-canonical) refrain, "Blessed be YHVH and blessed be His name forever and ever" and adds at the end of the Psalm the tag, "This is for a memorial". The Dead Sea Scrolls version also preserves a line beginning with the letter nun.

Psalm 145 is the last Psalm attributed explicitly to David, and also the last of the nine acrostic Psalms in its placement in the Book of Psalms (the acrostic Psalms being Psalms 9, 10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119 and 145). Methodist writer Joseph Benson notes that the king (David) praises "his king", "termed so by way of eminence: the King of kings, the God by whom kings reign".

The following is the Hebrew text of Psalm 145:

Every day will I bless thee; and I will praise thy name for ever and ever.
Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.

And men shall speak of the might of thy terrible acts: and I will declare thy greatness.
They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness, and shall sing of thy righteousness.
The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy.

All thy works shall praise thee, O LORD; and thy saints shall bless thee.
They shall speak of the glory of thy kingdom, and talk of thy power;

Blind Runner and Guide Prepare for Lagos City Marathon After Year of Training LAGOS. At 5 am on a humid Tuesday, two figures jog side by side along t
he Bar Beach promenade, joined at the wrist by a short orange tether. Chukwudi Okeke, 34, lost his sight to glaucoma eight years ago. Beside him runs his guide, Tobi Adesanya, a 28-year-old bank teller who v
olunteered to help him reach a goal he once thought impossible: finishing the Lagos City Marathon.

On Saturday, the pair will line up with about 50,000 other runners at the National Stadium in Surulere. If they finish, Okeke will become one of the first visually impaired Nigerians to complete the race. A Year in the Making Okeke began running in 2026 at the suggestion of a
friend from the Nigeria Association of the Blind. He was intro
duced to Adesanya through a Lagos running club, and the two started training together in January 2027. "The first time, we ran two kilometres and I fell twice," Okeke said, laughing. "Now we can do thirty." Their coach, Mrs Funke Olatunji, designed a 40-week plan built around three or four runs each week. She said the main challenge was not fitness but communication. "The guide has to describe everything, from potholes to puddles to people 

stepping out from bus stops," she said. "That takes concentration over many hours." The Plan for Race Day Olatunji has given the pair a detailed race-day plan: * Start near the back of the field to avoid crowding in the first kilometres.
* Run at an even pace of about 7
 minutes 30 seconds per kilometre. * Walk for one minute at every drink station to take water and electrolytes. 
* Adesanya calls out turns, kerbs and speed bumps ten metres before they arrive. *
 Stop immediately if either runner feels dizzy or develops cramp. Their target is to finish within the six-hour time limit. "Finishing is the victory," Okeke said. "The time does not matter." Support From the Community The race organisers have given the pair bibs marked with a special symbol so that marshals and other runners can recognise them, and a m
edical volunteer on a bicycle will accompany them for the second half of the course along the Lekki-Epe Expressway. Okeke's church in Ikeja has organised a group of supporters to cheer at the 30 kilometre point, where many runners struggle. A Larger Message

Okeke hopes his run will encourage other blind people in Nigeria to take up sport and show that disability does not have to mean exclusion. He wants to start a guided running group in Lagos next year and is looking for volunteer guides. "Running gave me back my independence," he said. "Every morning I wake up with a reason to go outside."
Adesanya, who had never run more than 10 kilometres before meeting Okeke, says the experience has changed him too. "I
 came to help him," he said. "But he has taught me more about patience than anyone I know."

Tommy Bell (born 11 November 1992) is an English rugby union player who plays for Benetton.

He began his career with Sale Sharks in the Aviva Premiership, but moved to London Wasps for the 2012/2013 season, playing alongside his brother Chris Bell. On 6 June 2014, Bell made his move to the RFU Championship as he signed a contract with Jersey. However, after a month with Jersey, Bell was granted early release from his contract since a top flight club made an approach to him where he would officially move to Leicester Tigers.

On 17 February 2016, Bell agreed to a long-term deal with London Irish from the 2016–17 season. He joined RFU Championship side Ealing Trailfinders for the 2019–20 season. In 2022 he played for Benetton in United Rugby Championship. After playing for England U18, from 2011 to 2012 Bell was named in the England U20 squad.

Summary of Supreme Court Judgment HR-2026-1482-A: Neighbour Dispute over Rooftop Solar Glare Norwegian Supreme Court, judgment of 3 September 2026. Summary prepared by Kjetil Røed, senior associate, Advokatfirmaet Fjordlys DA, for clients in the construction and energy sectors. Introduction The Supreme Court has for the first time ruled on whether reflected glare from rooftop solar panels can constitute an unlawful nuisance under the Neighbour Relations Act. The judgment provides useful guidance for property owners and installers, as residential solar installations have increased rapidly in Norway since 2022. Facts In 2023 the owners of a detached house in Stabekk, Bærum, installed 28 solar panels on the north-facing side of a shallow roof, angled to catch the low evening sun. The neighbours, whose livin

g room and terrace faced the panels across a distance of about 14 metres, complained that sunlight reflected from the panels caused strong glare on clear afternoons between April and August. The neighbours documented glare l
asting up to 90 minutes on some days and claimed that it made their terrace unusable in the evening. The neighbours sued, requesting that the panels be moved or covered with an anti-glare coating. The district court found for the neighbours, but the court of appeal reversed, holding that solar panels are a normal and socially desirable feature of modern housing.

Questions Before the Supreme Court

- Whether glare from solar panels falls within the scope of section 2 of the Neighbour Relations Act. - How the social benefit of renewable energy should be weighed against the inconvenience caused to neighbours. - Whether the expected or customary use of property in a residential area had changed with the spread of solar installations. The Court's Reasoning

The Court confirmed that glare can amount to an unreasonable or unnecessary nuisance under section 2, in the same way as noise or shading. It emphasised that the assessment must consider how common the type of installation is in the area, but held that the general public interest in renewable energy does no
t justify any degree of disturbance. In this case, the panels were placed on an unusual north-facing slope where reflection
towards the neighbouring house was foreseeable, and alternative placements on the south-facing roof section were available at modest additional cost. The Court noted that the
installer had not carried out any glare assessment and found that the nuisance was unnecessary, because
it could have been avoided by a different layout. Outcome The Court ruled in favour of the neighbours and ordered the owners to fit anti-glare panels or relocate the installation within six months. Legal costs were awarded to the neighbours for all three instances. Practical Implicatio
ns Installers should consider glare risk when panels face neighbouring windows at close range, particularly on unconventional orientations, and document the assessment in the project file.

Summary of Supreme Court Judgment HR-2026-1482-A: Neighbour Dispute over Rooftop Solar Glare

Norwegian Supreme Court, judgment of 3 September 2026. Summary prepared by Kjetil Røed, senior associate, Advokatfirmaet Fjordlys DA, for clients in the construction and energy sectors.

Introduction

The Supreme Court has for the first time ruled on whether reflected glare from rooftop solar panels can constitute an unlawful nuisance under the Neighbour Relations Act. The judgment provides useful guidance for property owners and installers, as residential solar installations have increased rapidly in Norway since 2022.

Facts

In 2023 the owners of a detached house in Stabekk, Bærum, installed 28 solar panels on the north-facing side of a shallow roof, angled to catch the low evening sun. The neighbours, whose living room and terrace faced the panels across a distance of about 14 metres, complained that sunlight reflected from the panels caused strong glare on clear afternoons between April and August. The neighbours documented glare lasting up to 90 minutes on some days and claimed that it made their terrace unusable in the evening.

The neighbours sued, requesting that the panels be moved or covered with an anti-glare coating. The district court found for the neighbours, but the court of appeal reversed, holding that solar panels are a normal and socially desirable feature of modern housing.

Questions Before the Supreme Court

- Whether glare from solar panels falls within the scope of section 2 of the Neighbour Relations Act.
- How the social benefit of renewable energy should be weighed against the inconvenience caused to neighbours.
- Whether the expected or customary use of property in a residential area had changed with the spread of solar installations.

The Court's Reasoning

The Court confirmed that glare can amount to an unreasonable or unnecessary nuisance under section 2, in the same way as noise or shading. It emphasised that the assessment must consider how common the type of installation is in the area, but held that the general public interest in renewable energy does not justify any degree of disturbance. In this case, the panels were placed on an unusual north-facing slope where reflection towards the neighbouring house was foreseeable, and alternative placements on the south-facing roof section were available at modest additional cost.

The Court noted that the installer had not carried out any glare assessment and found that the nuisance was unnecessary, because it could have been avoided by a different layout.

Outcome

The Court ruled in favour of the neighbours and ordered the owners to fit anti-glare panels or relocate the installation within six months. Legal costs were awarded to the neighbours for all three instances.

Practical Implications

Installers should consider glare risk when panels face neighbouring windows at close range, particularly on unconventional orientations, and document the assessment in the project file.

The French cruiser Wattignies was the lead ship of a class of two torpedo cruisers, the , that were built for the French Navy () in the early 1890s. The ship was the first in French Navy service to mount quick-firing (QF) guns. As well as five QF guns, the cruiser was fitted with four torpedo tubes. Launched in 1891 in Cherbourg, Wattignies was commissioned into the Mediterranean Squadron () as part of the reserve. The cruiser saw service in Crete from 1896, supporting French humanitarian and political objectives on the island. This proved to be the only active deployment that the ship would perform. In 1899, the ship was transferred to Rochefort, returning to the reserve. Wattignies remained in service for another eight years until being retired and, in 1908, struck from the naval register.

Design and description
The Wattignies-class cruisers were designed as enlarged and improved versions of the preceding by Louis de Bussy in 1888. The design was created in response to the 1884 publication (The Navy, its Past and its Future, Battleship and Torpedo boats), in which Minister of Marine, Auguste Gougeard, articulated his vision of the warship of the future. The ships measured overall and between perpendiculars, with a beam of and an average draft of , increasing to aft. Wattignies displaced . By 1904, this was listed as .

Wattignies was powered by two vertical triple-expansion steam engines, each driving a single propeller shaft, using steam provided by four coal-burning Admiralty boilers at a pressure of . The machinery was designed to produce a total of intended to give them a maximum speed of . Reported output was for a speed of . The cruiser carried of coal, which gave a range of at a speed of . The ship's complement amounted to 185 officers and enlisted men.

The main battery of the Wattignies class consisted of five 26.2-calibre M1881 QF guns. Two were located under the forecastle, two amidships on sponsons and one on the poop deck. July 20, 1969, and walked on the lunar surface, while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit in the command and service module (CSM), and all three landed safely on Earth in the Pacific Ocean on July 24. Five subsequent Apollo missions also landed astronauts on the Moon, the last, Apollo 17, in December 1972. In these six spaceflights, twelve people walked on the Moon. Apollo ran from 1961 to 1972, with the first crewed flight in 1968. It encountered a major setback in 1967 when an Apollo 1 cabin fire killed the entire crew during a prelaunch test. After the first successful landing, sufficient flight hardware remained for nine follow-on landings with a plan for extended lunar geological and astrophysical exploration. Budget cuts forced the cancellation of three of these. Five of the remaining six miss

ions achieved successful landings, but the Apollo 13 landing was prevented by an oxygen tank explosion in transit to the Moon, crippling the CSM. The crew barely returned to Earth safely by using the lunar module as 
a "
lifeboat" on the return journey. Apollo used t
he Saturn family of rockets as launch vehicles, which were also used for an Apollo Applications Program, which consisted of Skylab, a space station that supported three crewed missions in 1973–1974, and the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, a joint United States-Soviet Union low Earth orbit mission in 1975. Apollo set several major human spaceflight milestones. It stands alone in 
sending crewed missions beyond low Earth orbit. Apollo 8 was the first crewed spacecraft to orbit another celestial body, and Apollo 11 was the first c
rewed spacecraft to land humans on one. Overall, the Apollo program returned of lunar rocks and
 soil to Earth, greatly contributing to the understanding of the Moon's composition and geological history. The program laid the foundation for NASA's subsequent human spaceflight capability and funded construction of its Johnson Space Center and Kennedy Space Center. Apollo also spurred advances in many areas of technology incidental to rocketry and human spaceflight, including avionics, telecommunications, and computers. he felt "Apollo riding his chariot across the Sun was appropriate to the grand s
cale of the proposed program". The context of this was that the

It was the third US human spaceflight program to fly, preceded by the two-person Project Gemini conceived in 1961 to extend spaceflight capability in support of Apollo.

Kennedy's goal was accomplished on the Apollo 11 mission when astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed their Apollo Lunar Module (LM) on July 20, 1969, and walked on the lunar surface, while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit in the command and service module (CSM), and all three landed safely on Earth in the Pacific Ocean on July 24. Five subsequent Apollo missions also landed astronauts on the Moon, the last, Apollo 17, in December 1972. In these six spaceflights, twelve people walked on the Moon.

After the first successful landing, sufficient flight hardware remained for nine follow-on landings with a plan for extended lunar geological and astrophysical exploration. Budget cuts forced the cancellation of three of these. Five of the remaining six missions achieved successful landings, but the Apollo 13 landing was prevented by an oxygen tank explosion in transit to the Moon, crippling the CSM. The crew barely returned to Earth safely by using the lunar module as a "lifeboat" on the return journey. Apollo used the Saturn family of rockets as launch vehicles, which were also used for an Apollo Applications Program, which consisted of Skylab, a space station that supported three crewed missions in 1973–1974, and the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, a joint United States-Soviet Union low Earth orbit mission in 1975.

Apollo set several major human spaceflight milestones. It stands alone in sending crewed missions beyond low Earth orbit. Apollo 8 was the first crewed spacecraft to orbit another celestial body, and Apollo 11 was the first crewed spacecraft to land humans on one.

Overall, the Apollo program returned of lunar rocks and soil to Earth, greatly contributing to the understanding of the Moon's composition and geological history. The program laid the foundation for NASA's subsequent human spaceflight capability and funded construction of its Johnson Space Center and Kennedy Space Center. Apollo also spurred advances in many areas of technology incidental to rocketry and human spaceflight, including avionics, telecommunications, and computers.

Name
The program was named after Apollo, the Greek god of light, music, and the Sun, by NASA manager Abe Silverstein, who later said, "I was naming the spacecraft like I'd name my baby." Silverstein chose the name at home one evening, early in 1960, because he felt "Apollo riding his chariot across the Sun was appropriate to the grand scale of the proposed program".

The context of this was that the program focused at its beginning mainly on developing an advanced crewed spacecraft, the Apollo command and service module, succeeding the Mercury program. A lunar landing became the focus of the program only in 1961. Thereafter Project Gemini instead followed the Mercury program to test and study advanced crewed spaceflight technology.

Background

Origin and spacecraft feasibility studies

RailInfo Kiosk User Manual: Station Timetable Terminals, Vietnam Railways Southern Region This manual explains how passengers and station staff use the
touch-screen timetable kiosks installed at Saigon, Bien Hoa, Phan Thiet and Nha Trang stations in 2026. The kiosks were supplied by Hanseong Display Systems of Suwon under a contract with the Saigon Railway Transport Company. Overview of the Kiosk Each kiosk has a 32-inch touch screen, a small thermal printer and a QR code reader. It displays the full timetable for trains departing the station in the next 24 hours, along with platform numbers, expected delays and seat availability for each class. 
Information is updated every two minutes from the central dispatching system. Passengers can switch
 the interface between Vietnamese, English
, Korean and Chinese using the flag buttons at the top of the screen. Finding a Train From the home screen, touch Departures to see a list of upcoming trains sorted by departure time. Each row shows the train number, such as SE2 or SPT1, the destination, the scheduled time, the expected time and the platform. Trains running more than ten minutes late are highlighted in orange. To search for a specific destination, touch Search an
d type the first letters of the station name; the keyboard accepts Vietnamese with or without accents.

Reading a Train Detail Page Touching a train opens a detail page showing every stop with arrival and departure times. The page also lists the following information:

- Available seat and berth classes, such as soft seat, six-berth hard sleeper and four-berth soft sleeper. - Remaining places in each class, updated from the ticketing system. - Whether a dining car is attached to the train. - Any service notices, such as engineering works between Muong Man and Thap Cham. Printing a Timetable Passengers can print a short timetable for any train by touching Print on the detail page. The printout lists all stops and times and includes a QR code linking to live updates on the Vietnam Railways website. Printing is free but limited to three printouts per session to prevent waste. Station staff should refill paper rolls when the screen shows a low paper warning; spare rolls are kept in the locked compartment below the screen, opened with the staff key.

Using the QR Reader Passengers who bought tickets online can scan the QR code on their e-ticket to see their train's current status, carriage number and the platform position where their carriage will stop. This feature was suggested by Ms. Phan Ngoc Tram, customer service manager at Saigon station, after passengers with heavy luggage struggled to find their carriages on long trains. Troubleshooting for Staff If the screen freezes, hold the power button on the side for ten seconds to restart. If information appears out of date by more than ten minutes, check the network cable at the back of the kiosk and report the fault to the IT helpdesk. Hardware faults are handled by the supplier's service engineer in Ho Chi Minh City, Mr. Song Woo-jin, who visits each station monthly.

Proposal to the Digital Infrastructure Fund of the Province of Limburg

Applicant: Regionaal Historisch Centrum Limburg, Maastricht. Contact person: Rik Schoenmakers, head of information management. Amount requested: 96,500 euros. Duration: 14 months, starting January 2027. Project Summary

Our archive serves more than 30,000 online visitors each year who search notarial deeds, civil registration records and parish registers from the whole province. All of this metadata is st
ored in a database system that was built in-house in 2006 on an Oracle platform. The vendor will end extended support for our version in December 2027, the two developers who understood the original schema have retired, and every change now depends on an external consultant at high hourly rates. We request funding to migrate the collection database to an open-source PostgreSQL platform with a documented data model aligned with the national archival standards. Scope of the Migration The current database holds roughly 4.7 million records in 212 tables. Many of these tables are no longer used, and some contain duplicated person names entered by volunteers over the years. The migration will therefore not be a simple copy. It will consist of the following work packages: • An inventory of all tables, fields and dependencies, with a decision for each on whether to keep, merge or archive it • Design of a new data model compatible with the Records in Contexts standard • Development and testing of conversion scripts, run first on a full copy of production data • Deduplication of person and place names, supported by the volunteer team in Venlo
• Switchover to the new platform during a planned weekend outage, followed by a two-month parallel monitoring period

Risks and Mitigation

The greatest risk is loss or corruption of data during conversion. To reduce it, every conversion run will be followed by automated comparison of record counts and checksums, and a team of three archivists led by Marleen Houben will manually check a sample of 2,000 records spread across all collection types. The old system will remain available in read-only mode for six months after switchover.

A second risk is the limited availability of skilled staff. We have therefore agreed with the Open Archives cooperative in Leeuwarden, which completed a similar migration in 2024, that one of their developers, Tjerk Hoekstra, will review our design and conversion scripts at three fixed milestones. Benefits

Once completed, the migration will remove licence costs of approximately 28,000 euros per year, allow our own staff to maintain the database, and make it possible to exchange records with other Dutch archives through standard interfaces. Researchers
will notice faster searches and, after deduplication, more reliable results when tracing individuals across different record types.

Budget The requested amount covers a developer for twelve months at 0.8 FTE, consultancy from Open Archives, temporary server capacity for testing, and training for archive staff. The centre contributes staff time valued at 41,000 euros.

Oskar Dieter Alex von Rosenberg-Redé, 3rd Baron von Rosen
berg-Redé (4 February 1922 – 8 July 2004), also known as Alexis, Baron de Redé, was a prominent French banker, aristocrat, aes
thete, collector, and socialite. In 2003, he was appointed a commandeur of the Ordre 
des Arts et des Lettres for his restoration of the Hôtel Lambert, where he was known for hosting opulent costume balls. Involved in horse racing, in 1972 he won the Prix de Diane and came in second at the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe. Early life and education
Oskar Dieter Alex von Rosenberg-Redé was born in Zurich, Switzerland on
4 February 1922, the third 
and youngest chi
ld of (1878–1939), a banker from Austria-Hungary. His father 
– whose mother was Hungarian and father unknown – had been adopted by a banker named Rosenberg and made a citizen of Liechtenstein, then created a baron in the Hungarian nobility by the Emperor of Austria in 1916. Redé's mother was Edith von Kaulla (1890—1931), a member of an ennobled German Jewish family that had been part-owners of the Royal Württemberg Court Bank (″Königlich Württembergische Hofbank″, founded by Karoline Kaulla and Raphael Kaulla). He had two siblings. Born in 1919, his brother Hubert von Rosenberg-Redé was the heir to the barony, while his sister Marion von Rosenberg-Redé (born 1916) was handicapped.

The children were brought up Protestant and raised in a
 16-room hotel suite at the Dolder Grand Hotel in Zurich, attended by a great many maids, nannies, porters, and valets. Their father visited occasionally. As their finances decreased with the onset of World War II, they moved into a tw
o-bedroom suite. 
Diagnosed with leukemia, their mother died in 1931, when Redé was nine years old. Redé and his brother were then sent to be educated together at Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland.

On account of bankruptcy, his father committed suicide in 1939 at the family's estate (Villa Rosin) in the Austrian town of Kaumberg. Living on an insurance policy income
 of $200 a month, Redé moved to New York City, where he bri
efly attempted to acquire American citizenship. He traveled to California to work for an antique dealer, where he earned money to support his sister and befriended Elsie de Wolfe (known as Lady Mendl), as well as Salv
ador and Gala Dalí. He retur
ned

 in New York in 1941. His brother committed suicide in 1942 in Hollywood, California, whereupon Redé became the third and last Baron von Rosenberg-Redé, which was typically abbreviated as Baron de Redé in France. Career and later

 life

Entry into Parisian society In a New York restaurant, the 19-year-old Redé caught the eye of businessman Arturo López Willshaw and they became lovers in 1941. A married Chilean millionaire, Lopez-Willshaw (1900–62) lived with his wife Patricia Lopez Huici in a lavishly decorated house in Neuilly, France and was "famous 
for his extravagant cost
ume entertainments." Shortly after they became a couple, Lopez-Wilshaw

allegedly offered Redé $1 million to return with him to France, with Redé initially demurring. Upon Lopez-Willshaw's urging, in 1946 Redé moved to Paris in the entourage of Lady Mendl, an interior decorator ret

Oskar Dieter Alex von Rosenberg-Redé, 3rd Baron von Rosenberg-Redé (4 February 1922 – 8 July 2004), also known as Alexis, Baron de Redé, was a prominent French banker, aristocrat, aesthete, collector, and socialite. In 2003, he was appointed a commandeur of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres for his restoration of the Hôtel Lambert, where he was known for hosting opulent costume balls. Involved in horse racing, in 1972 he won the Prix de Diane and came in second at the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.

Early life and education
Oskar Dieter Alex von Rosenberg-Redé was born in Zurich, Switzerland on 4 February 1922, the third and youngest child of (1878–1939), a banker from Austria-Hungary. His father – whose mother was Hungarian and father unknown – had been adopted by a banker named Rosenberg and made a citizen of Liechtenstein, then created a baron in the Hungarian nobility by the Emperor of Austria in 1916. Redé's mother was Edith von Kaulla (1890—1931), a member of an ennobled German Jewish family that had been part-owners of the Royal Württemberg Court Bank (″Königlich Württembergische Hofbank″, founded by Karoline Kaulla and Raphael Kaulla). He had two siblings. Born in 1919, his brother Hubert von Rosenberg-Redé was the heir to the barony, while his sister Marion von Rosenberg-Redé (born 1916) was handicapped.

The children were brought up Protestant and raised in a 16-room hotel suite at the Dolder Grand Hotel in Zurich, attended by a great many maids, nannies, porters, and valets. Their father visited occasionally. As their finances decreased with the onset of World War II, they moved into a two-bedroom suite. Diagnosed with leukemia, their mother died in 1931, when Redé was nine years old. Redé and his brother were then sent to be educated together at Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland.

On account of bankruptcy, his father committed suicide in 1939 at the family's estate (Villa Rosin) in the Austrian town of Kaumberg. Living on an insurance policy income of $200 a month, Redé moved to New York City, where he briefly attempted to acquire American citizenship. He traveled to California to work for an antique dealer, where he earned money to support his sister and befriended Elsie de Wolfe (known as Lady Mendl), as well as Salvador and Gala Dalí. He returned in New York in 1941. His brother committed suicide in 1942 in Hollywood, California, whereupon Redé became the third and last Baron von Rosenberg-Redé, which was typically abbreviated as Baron de Redé in France.

Career and later life

Entry into Parisian society
In a New York restaurant, the 19-year-old Redé caught the eye of businessman Arturo López Willshaw and they became lovers in 1941. A married Chilean millionaire, Lopez-Willshaw (1900–62) lived with his wife Patricia Lopez Huici in a lavishly decorated house in Neuilly, France and was "famous for his extravagant costume entertainments." Shortly after they became a couple, Lopez-Wilshaw allegedly offered Redé $1 million to return with him to France, with Redé initially demurring.

Upon Lopez-Willshaw's urging, in 1946 Redé moved to Paris in the entourage of Lady Mendl, an interior decorator returning to Versailles from California. Lopez-Willshaw's wife, a first cousin born Patricia Lopez-Huici, was cool towards her husband's companion, though the three often attended social events as a group and traveled together, moving between suites in European and American hotels, the house in Neuilly, a yacht (Gaviota IV), and an apartment in California. The Lopez-Wilshaws and Redé also took up organizing lavish costume balls together.

VaxPoint Mobile Clinic Kit: User Manual for Campaign Teams This manual is for vaccinators and recorders using the VaxPoint mobile clinic kit during the 2026 polio and measles supplementary immunisation campaign in Gia Lai and Kon Tum provinces. The kit was supplied by the Korea International Cooperation Agency and assembled by MedLog Asia in Incheon. Read sections 1 to 3 before your first session day.

1 What Is in the Kit Each kit arrives in two hard cases. Case A holds the cold chain equipment and case B holds the recording equipment and supplies. Check the contents against the list taped inside each lid before leaving the dis

trict health centre:

* One solar direct-drive vaccine carrier with a 4.2-litre storage compartment and a digital temperature display. * Two backup cold boxes with 16 frozen ice packs. * One rugged tablet preloaded with the campaign registration app and a spare power bank. * A folding table, two stools, a shade canopy and four weighted pegs. * Sharps disposal boxes, cotton wool, finger markers and tally sheets as paper backup. 2 Setting Up a Session Site Choose a shaded, flat spot near the village meeting house or school, ideally with space for a queue that does not block the entrance. Unfold the table so that the vaccinator faces the queue and the recorder sits at the end where children leave. Place the vaccine carrier behind the vaccinator, out of direct sun, with the display facing upward so that it can be read without opening the lid. The carrier should show between 2 and 8 degrees before any vial is removed. 3 Keeping Vacci
nes Cold

The solar carrier maintains temperature for up to five days with
out sun once its internal ice lining has frozen. On cloudy days in the highlands, check the display every hour and record readings on the temperature log. If the display re
ads above 8 degrees for more than 30 minutes, stop vaccinating, move vials to a backup cold box and call your supervisor. Oral polio vaccine vials carry a vaccine vial monitor on the label; do not use any vial where the inner square is the same colour as or darker than the outer circle. 4 Recording Doses Each child is registered on the tablet with name, date of birth and village. The app works offline and uploads records when the tablet
 reaches network coverage. Mark the child's left little finger with the marker after each oral polio dose so that teams can identify 
vaccinated children during house-to-house checks. If the tablet fails, use the paper tally sheets and enter the data at the district office the same evening. 5 Packing Up Return unopened vials to the carrier, count used vials and record
the number. Seal sharps boxes when three-quarters full. Clean the table with the supplied wipes. Report any damaged equipment to the district logistics offi
cer, Mr. Ksor Hlinh in Pleiku or Ms. Y Thao in Kon Tum, who can arrange replacement parts through the KOICA field office managed by Mr. Jeon Hyun-woo.

ohns Hopkins School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland. Lane served as the head of the Department of Biological Ch
emistry from 1978 to 1997, was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1987, and was named a University Distinguished Service Professor – the institution's highest academic title – in 2001. oles in the American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, most notably serving as the society's president in 1990. emistry. His interest in vitamins and nutrition led him to focus later on lipogenesis an

Personal life Lane met and married his wife Patricia during his time at Iowa State. The couple had two children Danny Lane and Claudia Lane. ing on the Chesapeake Bay. He was involved in local social justice and environmental activism. Lane died of myeloma on April 10, 2014.

Testing Garden Soil pH with a Home Kit and a Glass of Vinegar Before you buy lime, sulphur or a new bag of compost for your vegetable beds, it pays to know what your soil actually needs. This tutorial, prepared by the allotment association of Novi Zagreb, walks you through a simple pH test using an inexpensive kit from a garden centre, plus two kitchen tests for carbonate and texture. The whole process takes about an hour, most of it waiting for soil to settle. Collecting a Good Sample A test is only as reliable as the sample. Soil varies from one corner of a plot to another, so take several small samples and mix them. Here is how: - Choose a dry day, at least a week after you last added fertiliser or compost. - Remove surface mulch and dig a small hole about 15 centimetres deep with a clean trowel. - Take a thin slice of soil from the side of the hole, top to bottom. - Repeat in eight to ten spots across the bed, walking in a zigzag pattern. - Mix everything in a clean plastic bucket and remove stones, roots and worms.

Let the mixed sample dry indoors on newspaper for a day if it is very wet, because wet soil gives less reliable readings with most kits. Running the pH Test Most garden centre kits, such as the one sold by Agrocentar in Zagreb for about 12 euros, use a coloured indicator solution. Fill the test tube with soil to the first line, add the powder capsule, then add distilled water up to the second line. Do not use tap water, since Zagreb's water is quite hard and can raise the reading. Shake well for a minute and let the soil settle for at least half an hour, then compare the colour of the liquid against the chart on the box, holding it against a white background in daylight. Most vegetables grow well between pH 6.0 and 7.0. Potatoes and blueberries prefer more acidic soil, while brassicas such as cabbage and kale do better near 7.0. Checking for Carbonate

Put a teaspoon of dry soil 

on a saucer and pour a few drops of white vinegar over it. If it fizzes clearly, the soil contains free calcium carbonate and almost certainly has a pH above 7. In that case, never add lime. Many plots along the Sava river, where the soil is built on alluvial gravel, react this way.

What to Do With Your Results

If your pH is below 6, add garden lime in autumn at the rate printed on the bag, usually 150 to 300 grams per square metre, and test again next year. If it is abo
ve 7.5, work in compost rather than trying to acidify with chemicals. For anything unusual, the association's soil volunteer, Branko 

Lovrić, can arrange a laboratory test at the Faculty of Agriculture for a small fee.

Basile Khoury, BS (15 August 1900, Borj-Safita, today Syria – 22 April 1985) was the first Archeparch of the Melkite Greek Catholic Archeparchy of Sidon in Lebanon.

Life
Basile Khoury was ordained priest on May 2, 1928 and became Chaplain of the Melkite Basilian from the Holy Redeemer (BS). He was named to the Eparchy of Sidon, being appointed on 15 March 1947 at 25 March 1947 ordained to the episcopate. At the beginning of the 1960s during his tenure and under his patronage was erected a hexagonal chapel in Maghdouché, a Lebanese pilgrimage center, and this chapel had 28 meter high with a statue of "Our Lady of Mantara". Khoury was a Council Father during the first and second sessions of the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965).

On November 18, 1964, the Eparchy of Sidon was elevated to Archeparchy by Pope Paul VI and Khoury was appointed Archbishop of Sidon. On 30 July 1965 he was co-consecrator of the Archbishop Georges Haddad. On reaching the age limit, he was, at the same time appointed with 77 years on August 25, 1977 Titular Bishop of Myra of Greek Melkites and until his death on April 22, 1985 became Archbishop Emeritus of Sidon.

Reducing Time to Hire for Nursing Staff at Gdańsk University Hospital Technical report of the Human Resources Department. Authors: Iwona Zalewska, recruitment manager, and Bartłomiej Kasprzak, HR analyst. Covering the period January 2025 to June 2026. 1 Context In 2024 the hospital took an average of 71 days to fill a vacant nursing position, measured from the date the vacancy was approved to the date the new nurse started work. During that time, wards relied on overtime and agency staff, at an estimated additional cost of 4.2 million złoty for the year. Exit interviews with candidates who withdrew showed that many accepted offers from other hospitals in the Tricity area while waiting for our decision. In January 2025 the hospital introduced a revised hiring process for nurses, and this report evaluates its effects over eig
hteen months. 2 Changes Introduced

The revised process differed from the previous one in several ways: - Vacancies are advertised continuously for common roles instead of being posted one at a time.
- Ward managers interview candidates within five working days of application, using a standard interview guide. - Occupational health checks are scheduled on the day of the interview, rather than after the offer.
- Offers are made within 48 hours of the interview, with salary determined from a published grid. - Onboarding begins with a fixed monthly start date, allowing group induction. 3 Results Between January 2025 and June 2026 the hospital hired 214 nurses. Median time to hire fell from 71 days to 34 days. The share of candidat
es who withdrew after interview decreased from 23 percent to 9 percent. Agency spending on nursing shifts fell by 38 percent compared with 2024, although part of this reduction also 
reflects the opening of a new nursing programme at the Medical University of Gdańsk, which increased the supply of graduates in summer 2025. Retention after one year was 86 percent for nurses hired under the new process, compared with 81 percent for those hired in 2023 and 2024. Ward managers rated the new hires similarly to previous cohorts in their six-month evaluations. 4 Problems Encountered

The continuous advertising approach created high application volumes for surgical and internal medicine wards but very few for psychiatry and long-term care, where vacancies remained open for an average of 58 days. Some ward managers found it difficult to schedule interviews within five days during periods of high workload, and the target was met in only 74 percent of cases. Occupational health capacity also became a bottleneck in September 2025, when 31 graduates applied in the same fortnight. 5 Recommendations The hospital should keep the revised process and extend it to midwives and medical laboratory staff. For hard-to-fill specialties, targeted measures are needed, such as partnerships with nursing schools in Słupsk and Elbląg and a relocation allowance. HR should also arrange backup interviewers from a pool of senior nurses to support ward managers during busy periods.

1 Context

In 2024 the hospital took an average of 71 days to fill a vacant nursing position, measured from the date the vacancy was approved to the date the new nurse started work.
