Exit interviews with candidates who withdrew showed that many accepted offers from other hospitals in the Tricity area while waiting for our decision. In January 2025 the hospital introduced a revised hiring process for nurses, and this report evaluates its effects over eighteen months.

2 Changes Introduced

The revised process differed from the previous one in several ways:

- Vacancies are advertised continuously for common roles instead of being posted one at a time.
- Ward managers interview candidates within five working days of application, using a standard interview guide.
- Occupational health checks are scheduled on the day of the interview, rather than after the offer.
- Offers are made within 48 hours of the interview, with salary determined from a published grid.

The continuous advertising approach created high application volumes for surgical and internal medicine wards but very few for psychiatry and long-term care, where vacancies remained open for an average of 58 days. Some ward managers found it difficult to schedule interviews within five days during periods of high workload, and the target was met in only 74 percent of cases. Occupational health capacity also became a bottleneck in September 2025, when 31 graduates applied in the same fortnight.

5 Recommendations

The hospital should keep the revised process and extend it to midwives and medical laboratory staff. For hard-to-fill specialties, targeted measures are needed, such as partnerships with nursing schools in Słupsk and Elbląg and a relocation allowance. HR should also arrange backup interviewers from a pool of senior nurses to support ward managers during busy periods.

3 Results 3.1 Thermal History at the Study Sites Between December 2024 and May 2025, loggers deployed at 4 metres depth on the reefs of Tamandaré recorded a maximum daily mean temperature of 30.4 degrees Celsius, reached on 19 March. Degree heating weeks, calcu
lated from the local maximum monthly mean of 28.6 degrees, peaked at 7.2 in early April at the inner reef site and at 5
.8 at the outer site. Th
e difference reflects the greater exchange with cooler offshore water at the outer edge, where the loggers also showed larger daily temperature swings. 3.2 Bleaching Prevalence by Species Of 1,148 colonies tagged in November 2024, 1,092 were relocated in all three subsequent surveys. Bleaching responses differed markedly among the five most abundant species: • Millepora alcicornis bleached earliest, with 78 percent of colonies pale or white by mid-March
• Mussismi
lia harttii reached 52 percent bleached
 at the April peak • Siderastrea stellata showed partial paling in 41 percent of colonies but rarely complete whitening • Montastraea cavernosa bleached in 29 percent of c
olonies, mostly at the inner site • Favia gravida remained largely unaffected, with only 9 percent showing any paling Colony size had no significant effect on bleaching probability for any species exc
ept Mussismilia harttii, in which c
olonies larger than 40 centimetres in diameter were less likely to bleach than smaller ones (logistic regression, p = 0.013). We discuss possible explanations for this pattern in section 4. 3.3 Recovery and Mortality By the May survey, conducted after temperatures had fallen below 29 degrees for three consecutive weeks, most bleached colonies of Siderastrea and Montastraea had regained visible pigmentation. Recovery was slower in Mussismilia harttii, and 14 p

ercent of its tagged colonies showed partial tissue loss. Mortality was highest in the hydrocoral Millepora, where 31 percent of colonies had died completely and were already being overgrown by turf algae. 3.4 Site Comparison Total mortality across all species was 11.6 percent at the inner site and 4.3 percent at the outer site. When the two sites were compared using a generalised linear mixed model with species as a random effect, site remained a significant predictor of mortality even after accounting for maximum degree heating weeks. This suggests that factors beyond temperature contribute to the difference. Turbidity readings collected by Dr. Mariana Vasconcelos during the same period were roughly twice as high at the inner site, consistent with sediment runoff from the Rio Formoso estuary, and we consider this the most likely additional stressor.

Between December 2024 and May 2025, loggers deployed at 4 metres depth on the reefs of Tamandaré recorded a maximum daily mean temperature of 30.4 degrees Celsius, reached on 19 March. Degree heating weeks, calculated from the local maximum monthly mean of 28.6 degrees, peaked at 7.2 in early April at the inner reef site and at 5.8 at the outer site. The difference reflects the greater exchange with cooler offshore water at the outer edge, where the loggers also showed larger daily temperature swings.

3.2 Bleaching Prevalence by Species

Of 1,148 colonies tagged in November 2024, 1,092 were relocated in all three subsequent surveys. Bleaching responses differed markedly among the five most abundant species:

• Millepora alcicornis bleached earliest, with 78 percent of colonies pale or white by mid-March
• Mussismilia harttii reached 52 percent bleached at the April peak
• Siderastrea stellata showed partial paling in 41 percent of colonies but rarely complete whitening
• Montastraea cavernosa bleached in 29 percent of colonies, mostly at the inner site
• Favia gravida remained largely unaffected, with only 9 percent showing any paling

Colony size had no significant effect on bleaching probability for any species except Mussismilia harttii, in which colonies larger than 40 centimetres in diameter were less likely to bleach than smaller ones (logistic regression, p = 0.013). We discuss possible explanations for this pattern in section 4.

3.3 Recovery and Mortality

By the May survey, conducted after temperatures had fallen below 29 degrees for three consecutive weeks, most bleached colonies of Siderastrea and Montastraea had regained visible pigmentation. Recovery was slower in Mussismilia harttii, and 14 percent of its tagged colonies showed partial tissue loss. Mortality was highest in the hydrocoral Millepora, where 31 percent of colonies had died completely and were already being overgrown by turf algae.

3.4 Site Comparison

Total mortality across all species was 11.6 percent at the inner site and 4.3 percent at the outer site. When the two sites were compared using a generalised linear mixed model with species as a random effect, site remained a significant predictor of mortality even after accounting for maximum degree heating weeks. This suggests that factors beyond temperature contribute to the difference. Turbidity readings collected by Dr. Mariana Vasconcelos during the same period were roughly twice as high at the inner site, consistent with sediment runoff from the Rio Formoso estuary, and we consider this the most likely additional stressor.

The Arthur Ashe Monument is a bronze sculpture by Paul DiPasquale installed along Richmond, Virginia's Monument Ave
nue. The statue depicts tennis player Arthur Ashe, who was born, r
aised and buried in Richmond. Description The statue is situated on a 1
6-foot granite pedestal on a traffic island, at the intersection of Monument Avenue and Roseneath Road. The 12-foot tall bronze sculpture depicts Arthur Ashe holding a tennis racket in one hand and books in the other, surrounded by children. The books are raised higher than the tennis racket; this was requested by Ashe himself, as he tended to emphasize education over sports. Ashe's depiction faces west and the children face east. Background Arthur Ashe Ashe was born at
Richmond's St. Philip Hospital for Negroes on March 10, 1943. During his childhood, Richmond was segregated, and he was denied entry to tennis tournaments and was not allowed to practice on the city's best courts. In 1960, Ashe moved to St. Louis to attend Sumner High School. In the following years, Ashe would become the first player selected to the United States Davis Cup team (1981), and was the only black man to win the singles title at the US Open (1968), the Australian Open (1975), and Wimbledon (1975) tennis t

ournaments. He retired in April 1980. Following his death of AIDS-related pneumonia on February 6, 1993, Ashe's bod
y laid in

state at Virginia's Executive Mans
ion, located in Richmond. Monument Avenue At the time of the statue's construction, Monument Avenue had statues of several Generals of the Confederate States Army, as well as Confederate States Navy Commander Matthew Fontaine Maury and Confederate President Jefferson Davis. Among tallest were the Robert E. Lee Monument, which stood 21 feet tall atop a 40-foot pedestal, and the Davis Memorial, which sat on a 65-foot column. The monuments, constructed from 1890 to 1929, were likely influenced by the then-popular belief that the Confederacy was just and heroic, an ideology also referred to as the Lost Cause of the Confederacy. History DiPasquale met Ashe in 1992, and received permission to design

a statue of him. Nine crayon and pencil studies of Ashe were created before his death in 1993. Following his death, Ashe's widow Jeanne Moutoussamy-Ashe approved the studies, and recommended Virginia Heroes Incorporated for funding. The designs were first unveiled, in plaster form, in December 1994 at the Ashe Center. With the urging of City Manager Robert Bobb, Richmond City Council approved the placement of the statue on Monument Avenue in June 1995. This decision was met with opposition by both black and white people, both objecting to its placement beside statues of Confederate generals. One alternative location, supported by Mayor Leonidas B. Young II,

was in the formerly whites-only Byrd Park. On July 17, city council held an eight hour long hearing on the location of the statue, eventually voting 7-0 in favor of the Monument Avenue location. Several council members said that the hearing changed their opinions on the matter, especially comments by Ashe's brother and widow. The groundbreaking was eventually held on August 15. 500 attended the event, and several people raised Confederate flags behind the stage.

QuickSep 12U Satellite Dispenser: Integration Guide for Customers

The QuickSep 12U dispenser, manufactured by Aerospace Mechanics Kufstein, holds and releases cubesats of up to 12 units and 24 kilograms during launch. It has flown on eleven missions since 2022 with no separation anomalies. This guide tells satellite teams what they need to prepare before shipping their spacecraft to our integration facility, and what happens during the integration and launch campaign.

Mechanical Interface

The dispenser uses a rail-based interface following the widely adopted 12U cubesat specification. Satellites slide into the dispenser on four rails and are held by a spring-loaded pusher plate at the rear and a door at the front. Your satellite's rails must have a hard anodised surface, and their dimensions must be within the tolerances stated in the interface control document. In our experience, about one in five customer satellites arrives with at least one rail slightly out of tolerance, most often because of paint or thermal tape applied near the rail edges.

Pre-Shipment Checklist

Please confirm each of the following before your satellite leaves your facility. Our integration engineer, Benedikt Rainer, will request written confirmation for every item:

* Rail dimensions measured with a calibrated gauge at five points along each rail, with results recorded.
* Total mass and centre of gravity measured and within the limits for the selected dispenser configuration.
* Deployment switches tested at least twenty times, keeping the satellite fully powered off while depressed.
* Remove-before-flight pin installed and its streamer clearly visible.
* Vibration test report at qualification or acceptance levels for the launch vehicle concerned.

If any item cannot be confirmed, contact us before shipping. Discovering a problem at the integration site rarely leaves time for a fix, since integration slots are usually only one or two days.

Integration Procedure

Integration takes place in our ISO class 8 clean room in Kufstein or, by arrangement, at the launch provider's facility. Our team performs a fit check with a rail gauge, then inserts the satellite with your representative present. The door is closed and the dispenser is mounted on a shaker for a short low-level vibration test to confirm that nothing has shifted. Finally, we photograph the closed dispenser and seal the access ports. From this point, the satellite cannot be accessed until it reaches orbit.

Separation Sequence

After the launch vehicle reaches the target orbit, the vehicle's flight computer sends a release signal to the dispenser. The door opens within 50 milliseconds, and the pusher plate ejects the satellite at a velocity of about 1.5 metres per second. Your satellite's deployment switches then close, starting its onboard timer. International guidelines require that antennas and solar panels are not deployed for at least 30 minutes after separation, so that the satellite cannot interfere with the launch vehicle.

Support

During the campaign, our support line is staffed around the clock. Questions about this guide can be sent to customer engineering manager Dr. Annika Würtenberger.

Reinstinden is a mountain in Lom Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. The tall mountain is located in the Jotunheimen
 mountains within Jotunheimen National Park. The mountain sits about northeast of the village of Øvre Årdal and about southwest of the village of Vågåmo. The mountain is surrounded by several other notable mountains including Høgtunga to the south; Storådalshøi to the southwest; Hinnotefjellet, Semeltinden, and Søre Hellstugutinden to the west; Nestsøre Hellstugutinden, Store Hellstugutinden, and Nørdre Hellstugutinden to the northwest; Store Memurutinden and Austre Memurutinden to the north; Blåbreahøe to the northeast; and Surtningssue and Raudhamran to the east. See also
List of mountains of Norway by height

In fact, Argentine annual consumption of beef has averaged per capita, approaching per capita during the 19th century; consumption averaged in 2007. Argentine cuisine is described as a blending of cultures, from the Indigenous peoples of Argentina who focused on ingredients such as humita, potatoes, cassava, peppers, tomatoes, beans, and yerba mate, to Mediterranean influences brought by the Spanish during the colonial period. This led to cultural blending of criollos (gauchos and early Spanish settlers), Indigenous, and sub-Saharan African (due to slave trading) in the cuisine. Later, this was complemented by the significant influx of Italian and Spanish immigrants to Argentina during the 19th and 20th centuries, who incorporated plenty of their food customs and dishes such as pizzas, pasta and Spanish tortillas.

Beef is a main part of the Argentine diet due to its vast production in the country's plains. In fact, Argentine annual consumption of beef has averaged per capita, approaching per capita during the 19th century; consumption averaged in 2007.

Beyond asado (the Argentine barbecue), no other dish more genuinely matches the national identity. Nevertheless, the country's vast area, and its cultural diversity, have led to a local cuisine of various dishes.

The great immigratory waves consequently imprinted a large influence in the Argentine cuisine, after all Argentina was the second country in the world with the most immigrants with 6.6 million, only second to the United States with 27 million, and ahead of other immigratory receptor countries such as Canada, Brazil, Australia, etc.

Argentine people have a reputation for their love of eating. Social gatherings are commonly centred on sharing a meal. Invitations to have dinner at home are generally viewed as a symbol of friendship, warmth, and integration. Sunday family lunch is considered the most significant meal of the week, whose highlights often include asado or pasta.

Another feature of Argentine cuisine is the preparation of homemade food such as French fries, patties, and pasta to celebrate a special occasion, to meet friends, or to honour someone. Homemade food is also seen as a way to show affection.

Argentine restaurants include a great variety of cuisines, prices, and flavours. Large cities tend to host everything from high-end international cuisine to bodegones (inexpensive traditional hidden taverns), less stylish restaurants, and bars and canteens offering a range of dishes at affordable prices.

History

Amerindians lived in Argentina thousands of years before European explorers arrived. They mostly lived off of agriculture, as well as hunting, gathering, and fishing. Generally, the most common crops at this time were maize, potatoes, common beans, quinoa, and squash.

The Argentinian native people could be divided in three groups based on their main modality of acquiring food:

Hunters and gatherers who inhabited the Patagonia, Pampa, and Chaco regions.
Farmers in the northwestern, Cuyo, and Cordoba's mountain regions who mostly grew squash, melons, and sweet potatoes. These groups had great influence from Andean-Incan tradition.
Farmers in the Mesopotamia plains who belonged to the guaraní culture.

Spanish settlers came to Argentina in 1536 and began building chacras where Amerindians would work to harvest the food. The arrival of Europeans brought Argentina into the Columbian Exchange, with ingredients from the Old World such as wheat, grapevine, figs, and several kinds of fruits being introduced to the country for the first time. It was also during the Spanish colonial period that cattle, goat, and pig farming were first introduced to Argentina, forming the foundation of the large Argentine beef industry.

Laforrest H. Thompson (January 6, 1848 – June 22, 1900) was a Vermont attorney and politician who served as President of the Vermont State Senate and a Justice of the Vermont Supreme Court. Biography Laforrest Holman Thompson was born in Bakersf
ield, Vermont, on January 6, 1848. He was educated at Kimball Union Academy, taught school while studying law, was admitted to the bar in 1871, and opened a practice in Irasburg. A Republican, Thompson served as Orleans County State's Attorney from 1874 to 1875, and county Judge of Probate from 1876 to 1881. In 1880 and 1882 Thompson was Irasburg's member of the Vermont House of Representatives. In 1884 Thompson was elected to the Vermont Senate. He served one term, 1884 to 1885, and was the Senate's President Pro Tem. In 1890 Thompso
n was again elected to the Vermont House of Representatives. In 1891 he was appointed to the Vermont Supreme Court, on which he served until his death.

Thompson died in Irasburg on June 22, 1900. He is buried in Irasburg Cemetery, Plot 350, Row U 32a. Thompson's son Frank D. Thompson also served on the Vermont Supreme Court. Frank Thompson was married to Mabel Miles, whose father Willard W. Miles was also an associate justice of the Vermont Supreme Court.

"Friend with Benefit" is the sixth episode of the twenty-seventh season of the American animated television series The Simpsons, and the 580th episode of the series overall. The episode was directed by Matthew Faughnan and written by Rob LaZebnik. It aired in the United States on Fox on November 8, 2015. Plot The episode opens with a short parody of the Disney short Feast entitled "Fat". Santa's Little Helper is fed scraps from the Simpsons' dinner table until he gets too fat and dies. He goes to Heaven and God offers him a choice between Fit Dog Heaven and Fat Dog Hell. Fat Dog Hell flashes a "Free Pizza" sign and Santa's Little Helper runs inside.

Homer sees a commercial for a self-lifting chair and becomes interested in buying one, but the $1,100 price dismays him. After Lenny and Carl suggest that he try to raise the money through crowdfunding, Homer posts a video that persuades the residents of Springfield to donate. He soon has enough to buy the chair and posts a follow-up video of himself enjoying it, but the townspeople become so enraged upon seeing his frivolous use of their money that they storm the Simpson house and destroy the chair. Meanwhile, at Springfield Elementary, Lisa tries to attract potential members for the school magic club. A girl named Harper Jambowski (voiced by Kristen Bell) becomes 
interested in signing up, and the two begin to spend time together. Lisa tries to calm Homer's anger about losing the chair by asking him to take her and Harper to an Australian boy band concert, for which Harper's father Mike has already bought tickets. Homer agrees, but is surprised to discover that the group's seats are in an expensive VIP skybox. Mike, a wealthy entrepreneur and owner of several businesses and sports teams, joins them in the box, and he and Homer strike up a friendship of their own.

On the way home, Lisa complains to Homer that Harper never let her talk during the show, but Homer persuades her to stay friends with Harper so she can enjoy all the luxuries of the Jambowskis' lifestyle. Harper invites Homer and Lisa to see a performance by David Copperfield, but again she stops Lisa from participating as the fathers enjoy themselves. As Lisa becomes disenchanted with Harper, Mike invites the Simpsons to spend a week on h
is private island. They decline at first due to the children needing to attend school, but Mike bribes Principal Skinner to close Springfield Elementary for a week so they can go.

Harper gives Lisa a fancy new bicycle, but Lisa sees it as an insult to the one she owns and feels that Harper is trying to control everything around her. Although their argument escalates, Lisa decides to remain friends with Harper so that the family can enjoy the island's comforts. When the girls begin fighting again during the trip, Homer reluctantly takes the family home early for Lisa's sake, commenting that no one who would treat her so badly deserves to be her friend.

During the credits, Homer ruefully says goodbye to the island's amenities as the family flies back to Springfield. Looking out the window, he and Lisa see that Bart is still on the island and has spelled out the message "So long suckers" on
the shore.

Production
In April 2015, Entertainment Weekly reported that Kristen Bell was cast as Harper, who is Lisa's new entitled friend. Executive producer Al Jean described the character as a good friend if one obeys her. Illusionist David Copperfield would also play himself in the episode.

Cultural references Lenny mentions the crowdfunding process to produce Zach Braff's 2014 film Wish I Was Here. The movie theater on the island is playing the film Back to the Future.

Reception "Friend With Benefit" scored a 1.5 rating and was watched by 3.48 million viewers, making the episode Fox's highest rated show of the night.

Renovation Log: Unit 1204, Harumi Tower Residences This log is kept by the project manager at Sumika Renovation for the kitchen refit in the apartment of Mr. and Mrs. Nozaki. It records every change to the agreed plan, the reason for it and its effect on cost and schedule, so that the owners and the building management office have a clear history. Entries are listed with the most recent first. Change 6 (Recorded 26 September 2026)

1. Moved the dishwasher from the left to the right of the sink 2. Replaced the planned undermount sink with an integrated stainless steel worktop and sink 3. Added a pull-out waste bin unit in place of the 300 millimetre drawer unit The dishwasher move followed a site check by plumber Hiroshi Kagawa, who found that the building's waste stack connection sits on the right-hand side and that routing the drain to the left would require a longer pipe run with insufficient fall. The integrated worktop was requested by Mrs. Nozaki after seeing a sample at the showroom in Toyosu; it removes a seam that can trap dirt but adds 132,000 yen and two weeks of lead time from the fabricator. Change 5 (Recorded 12 September 2026) 1. Upgraded the range hood to a model with a quieter motor
2. Changed the ceiling light from a single fixture to four recessed downlights 3. Added a dimmer switch beside the dining area entrance Mr. Nozaki works from home and was concerned about hood noise during evening video calls. The upgraded model is rated at 38 decibels on its lowest setting compared with 46 decibels for the original choice. The building management rules require ceiling work to be inspected before closing, so the change to recessed lights adds one inspection visit.

Change 4 (Recorded 29 August 2026) 1. Postponed start of demolition from 1 September to 15 September 2. Arranged protection of the shared corridor and lift interior
3. Notified neighbours on floors 11 to 13 of the revised dates The building management office asked that noisy work not overlap with the façade repair scheduled for early September, which already restricts lift use. Corridor protection is required by the management association whenever materials are carried through common areas, and the cost is included in the original quotation.

Summary of Effects

Following change 6, the total project cost stands at 3,860,000 yen including tax, an increase of 214,000 yen over the signed estimate. Completion is now expected on 31 October, two weeks later than originally planned, because of the worktop lead time. Mrs. Nozaki approved the revised figures by email on 27 September, and a copy has been filed with the contract documents.

5 Discussion

The analysis in Section 4 shows that the share of Lagos State local government budgets allocated to capital projects has fallen steadily since 2019, from an average of 34 percent to 21 percent in 2026, while recurrent spending on salaries and overheads has absorbed most of the growth in federal allocations. In this section we interpret these results, compare them with findings from other Nigerian states and consider what they imply for budget reform at the local level.

5.1 Interpreting the Decline in Capital Spending

Three explanations are consistent with our data. First, the expansion of local government payrolls after the 2019 minimum wage increase added fixed costs that councils could not easily reduce. Second, the share of revenue from the Federation Account that reaches local governments through the State Joint Local Government Account has been irregular, which makes councils reluctant to commit to multi-year projects. Third, internally generated revenue has remained small, rarely exceeding 12 percent of total revenue, so councils have little room to fund investment from their own resources.

Our interviews with treasurers in Ikorodu, Alimosho and Epe support the second explanation in particular. Several described receiving allocations weeks late or reduced without notice, and one, Mr Ganiyu Balogun, stated that his council "plans capital projects but executes only what the last two months of revenue can pay for." This short planning horizon helps explain why the projects that do proceed are mostly small, such as drainage cleaning and market stall repairs.

5.2 Comparison With Other States

Our findings are broadly in line with earlier studies of Kano and Rivers States, although the decline in Lagos is steeper. A distinctive feature of Lagos is the large number of Local Council Development Areas created in 2003, which share revenue with the original twenty local governments and multiply administrative costs. Several patterns emerge across the three states:

- Recurrent spending rises faster than total revenue in years following wage reviews.
- Capital budgets are approved at realistic levels but executed at less than half.
- Councils with stronger property rate collection sustain higher capital spending.
- Transparency in budget publication is associated with higher execution rates.

5.3 Policy Implications

If irregular transfers are the main obstacle, then reforms focused only on improving local revenue collection will have limited effect. A more predictable schedule of transfers, perhaps through a published monthly formula, could allow councils to plan investment with confidence. At the same time, councils that strengthen property tax administration, as Ikeja has done through its digital rates register, appear better able to protect capital budgets from fluctuations.

5.4 Limitations

Our data cover twelve of the fifty-seven councils and development areas in Lagos State, chosen for data availability rather than at random. Budget documents also record approved rather than actual spending for some years, which may overstate capital investment. Section 6 outlines how future work could address these gaps.

Hradištko is a municipality and village in Prague-West District in the Central Bohemian Region of the Czech Republic. It has about 2,400 inhabitants.

Administrative parts
Villages of Brunšov, Pikovice and Rajchardov are administrative parts of Hradištko.

Geography
Hradištko is located about south of Prague. It lies in the Benešov Uplands. The highest point is at above sea level. The municipality is situated at the confluence of the Vltava and Sázava rivers. The Štěchovice Reservoir, built on the Vltava, lies on the southern municipal border.

History
The first written mention of Hradištko is in a papal bull of Pope Clement V from 1310. The owners of the village often changed until 1636, when Hradištko was purchased by the Strahov Monastery.

Sights
The main landmark is the Hradištko Castle. There was a fortress from 1571, which was rebuilt into the current simple Baroque castle in 1709. Today the building houses the municipal office and a library.

Notable people
Magda Sonja (1886–1974), Austrian-American actress

Summary of Decision: Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, Case No. eI-3417-552/2026 Parties: Algirdas Mickevičius (applicant) against the Vilnius County Adam Mickiewicz Public Library (respondent). Decision delivered
 22 April 2026 by Judge Daiva Stankevičiūtė. 1 Facts

The applicant, a local historian, requested access to the library's internal catalogue records for a collection of interwar pamphlets acquired in 1998. The library's public online catalogue lists only 212 items from the collection, while an annual report from 2001 refers to "approximately 640 printed items." The applicant asked for the complete internal inventory, including acquisition notes and records of items withdrawn or transferred. The library refused, arguing that its internal cataloguing database is a working tool rather than an official document and that some notes contain personal data about donors. 2 Issues The court identified three questions for decision: - Whether internal catalogue records held by a public library are documents within the meaning of the Law on the Right to Obtain Information from State and Municipal Institutions. - Whether the pr
esence of donor personal data justifies refusing access to the entire record set. - Whether the library must explain the discrepancy between the publ
ished and internal counts. 3 Reasoning On the first question, the court held that a catalogue maintained by a publicly
funded library to manage publicly owned collections is information held in the course of a public function. The fact that staff use it daily as an operational tool does not change its character. The court noted that the library had itself relied on these records when preparing its annual reports, which undermin
ed the claim that they were merely informal drafts. On the second question, the court accepted that the names and addresses of private dono
rs were personal data protected under the General Data Protection Regulation. However, the library had not attempted partial disclosure. The court found that redacting donor details 
from the relevant fields would take limited effort and would leave the bibliographic and acquisition information intact. On the third question, the court declined to order an explanation. The right of access covers existing information, and an institution cannot be compelled to create new analysis or commentary in response to a request. 4 Outcome The refusal was annulled in part. The library must provide the internal catalogue records for the 1998 collection within twenty working days, with donor names and contact details redacted. Each party bears its own costs. The library may appeal to
 the Supreme Administrative Court of Lithuania within thirty days. 5 Significance The decision is likely to be
 cited in future requests concerning museum and archive inventories, which are often held in similar internal systems. Institutions should review whether their cataloguing databases can produce r
edacted extracts quickly, since a blanket refusal on data protection grounds is unlikely to survive review.

Summary of Decision: Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, Case No. eI-3417-552/2026

Parties: Algirdas Mickevičius (applicant) against the Vilnius County Adam Mickiewicz Public Library (respondent). Decision delivered 22 April 2026 by Judge Daiva Stankevičiūtė.

1 Facts

The applicant, a local historian, requested access to the library's internal catalogue records for a collection of interwar pamphlets acquired in 1998. The library's public online catalogue lists only 212 items from the collection, while an annual report from 2001 refers to "approximately 640 printed items." The applicant asked for the complete internal inventory, including acquisition notes and records of items withdrawn or transferred. The library refused, arguing that its internal cataloguing database is a working tool rather than an official document and that some notes contain personal data about donors.

2 Issues

The court identified three questions for decision:

- Whether internal catalogue records held by a public library are documents within the meaning of the Law on the Right to Obtain Information from State and Municipal Institutions.
- Whether the presence of donor personal data justifies refusing access to the entire record set.
- Whether the library must explain the discrepancy between the published and internal counts.

3 Reasoning

On the first question, the court held that a catalogue maintained by a publicly funded library to manage publicly owned collections is information held in the course of a public function. The fact that staff use it daily as an operational tool does not change its character. The court noted that the library had itself relied on these records when preparing its annual reports, which undermined the claim that they were merely informal drafts.

On the second question, the court accepted that the names and addresses of private donors were personal data protected under the General Data Protection Regulation. However, the library had not attempted partial disclosure. The court found that redacting donor details from the relevant fields would take limited effort and would leave the bibliographic and acquisition information intact.

On the third question, the court declined to order an explanation. The right of access covers existing information, and an institution cannot be compelled to create new analysis or commentary in response to a request.

4 Outcome

The refusal was annulled in part. The library must provide the internal catalogue records for the 1998 collection within twenty working days, with donor names and contact details redacted. Each party bears its own costs. The library may appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court of Lithuania within thirty days.

5 Significance

The decision is likely to be cited in future requests concerning museum and archive inventories, which are often held in similar internal systems. Institutions should review whether their cataloguing databases can produce redacted extracts quickly, since a blanket refusal on data protection grounds is unlikely to survive review.

Atyap Chiefdom is a Nigerian traditional state of the Atyap people, located on the upper Kaduna River basin of the central Nigeria plateau in the Middle Belt. Its headquarters is at A̠tak Njei, Zangon Kataf, southern Kaduna state, Nigeria. People History The Atyap Chiefdom was created in 1995. In 2007, it was upɡraded to a First Class status. Government The Atyap Chiefdom is run by the Atyap Traditional Council, with the A
̠gwatyap as its head. Administrative divisions Districts The Kaduna state Ministry of Local Government Affairs gave its number of Existing Districts as 16, Approved Districts as five and Approved Village Units as 61. These are the districts between 1995 and 2017: However, these are the current five Government-Approved Districts from 2017 onwards, trimmed down by the incumbent Kaduna State governor Nasir Elrufai who accordingly said, as reported by Premium Times, Nigeria that the committee set up to address the district administration in the state concluded that the proliferation
of the number of districts from the pre-2001 era had created a financial burden for Local Government Councils. Hence, their reversal back to the pre-2001 era. Viz:

Headquarters The headquarters of the Atyap Chiefdom is Atak Njei, where the Agwatyap'''s palace (Tyap: Magwatyap) is located. Of recent, there had been moves by the Nasir el-Rufai-led Kaduna State government to question the locating of the palace in that very region located at the outskirts of the Hausa-Fulani-Kanuri dominated town of Zangon Kataf (Tyap: Á̠nietcen-A̱fakan), a move which has strongly been countered by the Atyap Community Development Association (ACDA). The ruling monarchs of the Atyap Chiefdom are known as A̠gwatyap.

The word is derived from these two Tyap words: a̱gwam (i.e. a monarch) and A̱tyap'' (i.e. after the Atyap people) and literally means "monarch of the Atyap". Mary Margaret Grieve (11 April 1906 – 19 February 1998) was a Scottish magazine editor and journalist. She began her journalistic career working for local new
spapers and specialised magazines before being appointed editor of Woman magazine in 1937. Grieve was made its associate editor not long
after before returning to the position of editor in 1940, which she held until her early retirement in 1962. She led a group of editors who advised the Home Office on woman's duties during the Second World War. In retirement, Grieve authored two books offering tips for school-leaving girls and co-ran a Pâté making company. Biography Early life
Grieve was born at 3 Blackburn Road in

Ayr, Ayrshire on 11 Ap
ril 1906. She was the youngest daughter and the second child of the fundhold
er Robert Grieve and the n
urse Annie Craig, née Stark. Grieve spent most of her childhood bedridden due to illness, and was home-schooled until the age of 16, when she briefly attended a small Glasgow daily school, and then in Edinburgh. At age 17, she spent time in Switzerland, and went to a London secretarial college to learn shorthand and typing. Career Upon her return to Glasgow, Grieve sought independence, and worked on advertising for the Scottish Women's Rural Institutes's publication Scottish Home and County, and briefly edited the monthly magazine Scottish Nurse. She later worked as a freelancer for the next seven years for the women's picture paper The Bulletin, where she provided a new emphasis to women's features, and covered local happenings. Grieve authored the fictional book Without Alphonse: The Diary of a Frenchwomen in Scotland under the pseudonym "Ursula Mary Lyon" in 1935. In 1936, she heard from he
r younger brother and a friend of his of a vacancy, and was summoned to be interviewed in London. She made the editor of Woman monthly magazine that was first published in July 1937. Grieve became the associate editor of Woman the same year following its
owner Odhams Press bringing in the editor of Mother magazine to take over her former position. When the magazine's male editor joined the Royal Air Force in 1940, she once again was appointed editor. During the Second World War, Grieve led a group of editors who advised the Home Office on the role of women in the war. They argued against conscription women into the armed forces and persuaded the Home Office women contributed to the war effort by keeping communities and families united, and the men fighting for their wives and children would be demoralised if they believed their homes were divided. Grieve's lobbying led the government to exempt women from conscription. She and a friend used a stirrup pump while working as an air raid warden in London during The Blitz. Grieve's success as editor of Woman magazine was based on how she understood her audience and scarcely featured the wealthy and well-known figures since their community was different to others and inaccessible at the time. She featured practical advice for food and established practical departmen

ts to demonstrate and test goods in the post-austerity era. Grieve sought to reach as many women across the United Kingdom as possible and encouraged
 reader participation by letter or telephone. From 1952 to

 1960, she was a member of the Council for Industrial Design. Grieve was appointed to the
National Council for Diplomas in Art and Design in 1960
 and the council of the Royal College of Art three years later.

Training for a Marathon by Heart Rate, Not Pace Pace-based plans work beautifully on a flat, cool course, but runners who train in Colorado Springs or Santa Fe know that a 9:00 mile at 7,000 feet in July is a completely different effort from the same pace at sea level in November. Heart rate training solves this by measuring how hard your body is working rather than how fast your legs are moving. In this tutorial, you will set up
heart rate zones and use them to structure a marathon training plan.

Step 1: Find Your Numbers You need two measurements: resting heart rate and maximum heart rate. Measure resting heart rate first thing in the morning, before getting out of bed, on three consecutive days and take the average. For maximum heart rate, formulas based on age are often wrong by ten beats or more. A better approach is a field test: after a thorough warm-up, run three minutes hard uphill, jog down, then run another three minutes as hard as you can. The highest value your monitor records is a reasonable estimate. Step 2: Calculate Your Zones Use the heart rate reserve method,
 which accoun
ts for your fitness level. Subtract resting heart rate from maximum to get your reserve. Then calculate each zone as a percentage of the reserve plus the resting value. For a runner with a resting rate of 52 and a maximum of 188, the reserve is 136.

Calculate the zones as follows:

1. Zone 1, recovery, is 50 to 60 percent of reserve, or about 120 to 134 beats per minute in our example. 2. Zone 2, aerobic base, is 60 to 70 percent, or 134 to 147, where most training should happen. 3. Zone 3, marathon effort, is 70 to 80 percent, or 147 to 161. 4. Zone 4, threshold, is 80 to 90 percent, or 161 to 174
, used for tempo runs. 5. Zone 5, maximum effort, is above 90 percent and reserved for short intervals. Step 3: Structure Your Week A typical week includes three or four Zone 2 runs, one tempo session that spends twenty to forty minutes in Zone 4, and a long run mostly in Zone 2 with the final few miles in Zone 3. Total weekly time in Zones 4 and 5 should stay below about fifteen percent. Step 4: Watch for Cardiac Drift On long runs, especially in heat, heart rate
gradually climbs even when pace stays constant. This is called cardiac drift, and it is normal. Rather than maintaining pace, slow down to keep heart rate in the target zone. You may feel frustrated at first, but your pace
at the same heart rate will improve steadily over the training block. Step 5: Race Day

On race day, use heart rate as a guardrail for the first half, staying near the bottom of Zone 3. After halfway, run by feel, since heart rate becomes less reliable as fatigue builds.

A typical week includes three or four Zone 2 runs, one tempo session that spends twenty to forty minutes in Zone 4, and a long run mostly in Zone 2 with the final few miles in Zone 3. Total weekly time in Zones 4 and 5 should stay below about fifteen percent.

Step 4: Watch for Cardiac Drift

On long runs, especially in heat, heart rate gradually climbs even when pace stays constant. This is called cardiac drift, and it is normal. Rather than maintaining pace, slow down to keep heart rate in the target zone. You may feel frustrated at first, but your pace at the same heart rate will improve steadily over the training block.

Step 5: Race Day

On race day, use heart rate as a guardrail for the first half, staying near the bottom of Zone 3. After halfway, run by feel, since heart rate becomes less reliable as fatigue builds.

The International Convention for the Suppression of the Traffic in Women and Children is a 1921 multilateral treaty of the League of Nations that addressed the problem of international trafficking of women and children. Background
The growth of the social reform movement during the late 19th century gave momentum to international efforts by women's rights groups, social hygiene activists, and others, to address trafficking in women and children and its role in prostitution and labour exploitation. Previous international conventions had been ratified by 34 countries in 1901 and 1904, and 1910 as "Convention for Suppression of White Slave Trade". The League of Nations, formed in 1919, quickly became the organization coordinating international efforts to study and attempt to end the practice. The work of the League in this area is considered to be one of its successes while overall it was a failure due to its inability to prevent war. The work of the League in this area was a central part of Evelyn Waugh's 1928 novel Decline and Fall. League of Nations When it was established, the League of Nations at first did not include women's rights groups, who protested their exclusion and canvassed politicians for support. Ultimately, United States President Woodrow Wilson and France's Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau supported the participation of women's rights groups, who they argued were best suited to give a voice to women's issues. The League held the International Conference on White Slave Traffic in 1921, and agreed on the 1921 International Convention for the Suppression of the Traffic in Women and Children on 30 September 1921. In 1933, it passed the International Convention for the Suppression of the Traffic in Women of Full Age. Key contents The 1921 Convention
ensure that protection from trafficking and sexual exploitation on the international level. The Article 6 states that "The High Contracting Parties agree, in case they have not already taken licensing and supervision of employment agencies and offices, to prescribe such regulations as are required to ensure the protection of

women and children seeking employment in another country." and the Article 7 to "undertake in connection with immigration and emigration adopt such administrative and legislative measures as are required to check the traffic in women and children. In particular, they undertake to make such regulations as are required for the protection of women and children travelling on emigrant ships, not only at the points of departure and arrival, but also during the journey and to arrange for the exhibition, in railway stations and imports of notices warning women and children of the traffic and indicating the places where they can obtain accommodation and assistance." Impact The 1921 Convention set new goals for international efforts to stem human trafficking, primarily by giving the anti-trafficking movement further official recognition, as well as a bureaucratic apparatus to research and fight the problem. The Advisory Committee on the Traffic of Women and Children was a permanent advisory committee of the League. Its members were nine countries, and several non-governmental organizations. An important development was the implementation of a system of annual reports of member countries. Member countries formed their own centralized offices to track and report on trafficking of women and children. The advisory committee also worked to expand its research and intervention program beyond the United States and Europe. In 1929, a need to expand into the Near East (Asia Minor), the Middle East, and Asia were acknowledged. An international conference of central authorities in Asia was planned for 1937, but no further action was taken during the late 1930s.

Subject: Treno Amico app, date for the 2.0 launch and what we need from your stations

Dear Station Managers,

I am writing on behalf of the digital services team at Ferrovie della Calabria to confirm that version 2.0 of the Treno Amico passenger app will be released to the public on Monday 19 October. As you know, the new version adds mobile ticket purchase and real-time departures for every station on the netw
ork, which until now were available only on the website. Because this will change how many passengers interact with station staff, I want to make sure each of you knows what to expect. What Passengers Will Be Able to Do

With the new app, passengers can buy single tickets, return tickets and weekly passes, pay by card or with PostePay, and show the ticket on their phone to the conductor.
They can also see the next departures from any station, including delays reported by the control centre in Cosenza, and receive alerts if their usual train is cancelled. Season tickets for students and workers will move to the app in a later version, planned for the spring.

What Changes at Stations

• The QR codes printed on station noticeboards will open the app or its download page; new posters will arrive by courier the week before launch • Ticket machines continue to work as before, and paper tickets remain valid
• Conductors will carry handheld readers to check app tickets; the readers have already been distributed • Passengers may ask station staff for help installing the app, especially older people Training

We have prepared a short training session of forty-five minutes for station staff, which will run online on 7, 9 and 13 October at 15:00. Each station should send at least one person, ideally the staff member who works most often at the ticket counter. Please register through the link in the staff portal by 2 October. The session covers the basic features, how to answer the most common questions and what to do if a passenger's ticket does not appear.

Known Limitations

Some stations in the Sila area and on the Catanzaro Lido line have weak mobile coverage. Tickets bought in the app remain available offline once downloaded, but real-time information will not update without a signal. Please advise passengers to buy tickets before arriving at these stations.

If you have questions or concerns, contact me directly or write to the digital services mailbox. We will also hold a review call two weeks after the launch, on 2 November, to hear how the first days have gone at your stations and to collect feedback for the next update.
 Thank you for your help in making this launch a success. Best regards, Antonella Scarpelli, digital services coordinator

Training Local Technicians for Small Wind Turbine Upkeep in Marsabit County

Grant application to the Northern Kenya Energy Access Fund, submitted by the Laisamis Community Energy Trust, requested amount KSh 18,400,000 over 24 months.

1 Problem Statement

Between 2019 and 2023, donors and county programmes installed 46 small wind turbines of between 3 and 10 kilowatts at schools, dispensaries and water points across Laisamis, Loiyangalani and North Horr. A survey we carried out in May 2026 found that only 19 are still producing power. The rest have stopped because of failures that are usually simple to fix, such as seized yaw bearings, broken tail vanes, loose cables and blown charge controller fuses. No technician within 200 kilometres has the tools or training to carry out these repairs, and calling a contractor from Nairobi costs more than most institutions can pay.

The consequences are concrete. At Kargi dispensary the vaccine refrigerator now runs on a generator for only four hours a day, and two boreholes near Korr have returned to diesel pumping at a fuel cost of roughly KSh 22,000 per month each.

2 Project Objectives

The trust proposes to build a small, locally based maintenance service that can keep the existing turbines running and respond to faults within a week. Specifically, the project will:

1. Train twelve young people from the three wards as wind and solar maintenance technicians through a nine-month course with Meru National Polytechnic
2. Equip two mobile repair teams with a pickup truck, climbing gear, a tool set and an initial stock of spare parts
3. Repair or recommission at least 20 of the 27 idle turbines within the first year
4. Set up a service agreement with each institution, paid from savings on diesel, to fund the teams after the grant ends
5. Keep an online log of every turbine, its faults and its output, open to the county energy office

3 Approach

Trainees will be selected with the help of ward administrators, and at least half will be women, given that several of the water points are managed by women's groups. Classroom training in Meru will alternate with supervised field work on real turbines, so that repairs start as early as month three. Senior technician Abdi Halake, who maintained turbines for a mission hospital in Moyale for eleven years, will act as field supervisor.

4 Sustainability and Budget

Our modelling suggests that institutions currently spending on diesel can afford a monthly fee of KSh 4,500 for maintenance and still save money. With 30 sites under contract, the fee income would cover the salaries and running costs of both teams from the third year onward. The largest budget items are the vehicle at KSh 5.2 million, training fees at KSh 3.6 million and spare parts at KSh 2.9 million. A detailed budget and letters of support from the Marsabit county government and the Kargi and Korr water committees are attached.

Contact: Halima Guyo, Programme Director, Laisamis Community Energy Trust.

The Very Bad Book is a 2010 book of short stories for children written by Andy Griffiths and illustrated by Terry Denton. The Very Bad Book is the sequel to Griffiths and Denton's "The Bad Book" published in 2004. Griffiths has announced plans to release a third title in the series, The Super Bad Book, in 2011. Synopsis
Much like its predecessor, The Bad Book, which turned standard children's fairy tales and nursery rhymes on their head by rewriting them as the "bad" version, this book contains a number of tales that are "very bad". The characters are very bad, the illustrations are very bad, and the poems and jokes are all very bad, all with the aim of delighting the children (and their parents) who will read this book. There are 51 stories, poems, jokes, etc. in all. Reception The Logan Reporter called The Very Bad Book "... actually very good", noting that the trepidation some parents might feel at intr
oducing their children to such bad characters is unfounded as the book makes clear through its absurdity that these characters are bad and not to be emulated.

VėjoSargas Condition Monitoring Service: Getting Started for Wind Farm Operators VėjoSargas is a cloud service from Energetikos Analitika
 UAB, Kaunas, that collects vibration and operational data from wind turbines and alerts operators to developing faults in drivetrain components. This page explains what the 
service includes, how data are connected, and how alerts should be handled by maintenance teams. What the Service Monitors Ea
ch turbine is fitted with eight accelerometers mounted on 

the main bearing, gearbox stages and generator bearings, plus a speed sensor on the high-speed shaft. A small data unit in the nacelle samples vibration at up to
 25 kilohertz in short bursts several times an hour, when the turbine is operating within defined speed and power windows. The 
unit also reads temperatures, power output and wind speed from the turbine controller through its standard interface. Data are compressed and sent to our servers through the farm's existing fibre or mobile link. Our an
al
ysts and
algorithms look for characteristic frequency patterns associated with the most common drivetrain problems, including: * Outer and inner race damage in main and generator bearings. * Tooth wear and cracks in planetary and parallel gear stages. * Generator rotor imbalance and misalignment between gearbox
and generator. * Looseness in mountings and structural resonances. Connecting
 Your Turbines
 Installation is carried out by our field team or by a certified service partner. A typical installation t
akes one day per turbine and requires one stop of about four hours. Before installation, the operator must provide the turbine model and serial number, gearbox and bearing types, and network access details for the data unit. Supported turbine mod
els currently include most machines from Vestas, Nordex, Siemens Gamesa and Enercon in the 2 to 5 megawatt range. Alert Levels Alerts appear in the web dashboard and are sent by email. They follow a three-level scale. Level 1
indicates an early change that should be noted but needs no action beyond continued monitoring. Level 
2 means a developing fault has been identified, with a written recommendation such as an oil sample or borescope inspection within a specified period. Level 3 indi
cates advanced damage with a risk of secondary failure, and our analyst will contact the operator by phone within one
hour o
f confirmation. Reports and Integration Operators receive
a monthly report for each farm, summarising the condition of every turbine and listing open findings.
 Data can be exported in CSV format or connected to maintenance planning systems through our API. Several operators in Lithuania and Latvia feed alerts directly into their work order systems so that recommended inspections are scheduled automatically. Contract Terms The service is offered on three or five year co
ntracts, pr

iced per turbine per year. The price includes sensors, installation, data transmission, analysis and reports. For questions, operators can contact customer manager Paulius Jurkus at our Kaunas office during working hours.

Each turbine is fitted with eight accelerometers mounted on the main bearing, gearbox stages and generator bearings, plus a speed sensor on the high-speed shaft. A small data unit in the nacelle samples vibration at up to 25 kilohertz in short bursts several times an hour, when the turbine is operating within defined speed and power windows. The unit also reads temperatures, power output and wind speed from the turbine controller through its standard interface. Data are compressed and sent to our servers through the farm's existing fibre or mobile link.

Our analysts and algorithms look for characteristic frequency patterns associated with the most common drivetrain problems, including:

* Outer and inner race damage in main and generator bearings.
* Tooth wear and cracks in planetary and parallel gear stages.
* Generator rotor imbalance and misalignment between gearbox and generator.
* Looseness in mountings and structural resonances.

Connecting Your Turbines

Installation is carried out by our field team or by a certified service partner. A typical installation takes one day per turbine and requires one stop of about four hours. Before installation, the operator must provide the turbine model and serial number, gearbox and bearing types, and network access details for the data unit. Supported turbine models currently include most machines from Vestas, Nordex, Siemens Gamesa and Enercon in the 2 to 5 megawatt range.

Alert Levels

Alerts appear in the web dashboard and are sent by email. They follow a three-level scale. Level 1 indicates an early change that should be noted but needs no action beyond continued monitoring. Level 2 means a developing fault has been identified, with a written recommendation such as an oil sample or borescope inspection within a specified period. Level 3 indicates advanced damage with a risk of secondary failure, and our analyst will contact the operator by phone within one hour of confirmation.

Reports and Integration

Operators receive a monthly report for each farm, summarising the condition of every turbine and listing open findings. Data can be exported in CSV format or connected to maintenance planning systems through our API. Several operators in Lithuania and Latvia feed alerts directly into their work order systems so that recommended inspections are scheduled automatically.

Contract Terms

The service is offered on three or five year contracts, priced per turbine per year. The price includes sensors, installation, data transmission, analysis and reports. For questions, operators can contact customer manager Paulius Jurkus at our Kaunas office during working hours.

 head coach Gianluca Pezzotta and reviewed by sports physician Dr Silvia Arrigoni. Plan Version 4.2, Released 30 September 2026 1. Moved the first 30-kilometre long run in the sub-3:30 plan from week 11 to week 12. Runner feedback and
injury reports from the spring season showed a cluster of calf and Achilles complaints in weeks 11 and 12, and spreading the load gives one more week of adaptation. 
2. Added an optional strength session of twenty-five minutes on Mondays to all pl
ans, with video demonstrations of six
 exercises
. Strength work was previously mentioned only in the introduction, and few runners did it. 3. Reduced the number of interval sessions in the beginner plan from twelve to eight over eighteen weeks. Many beginners told us they found the interval days intimidating and skipped them, which defeated their purpose. 4. Corrected a pace table error in the sub-4:00 plan, where marathon pace was shown as 5:41 per kilometre instead of 5:40. Plan Version 4.1, Released 15 March 2026

1. Introduced heat guidance for spring marathons. When the forecast exceeds 22 degrees on a long run day, the app suggests running early in the morning and lowering target pace by 10 to 20 seconds per kilometre. 2. Added a cut-back week every fourth week to the sub

-3:00 plan, which had previously only reduced volume every fifth week. 3. Linked each plan to
the race calendar, so the taper starts automatically three weeks before the chosen race date. Should You Switch? If you are following version 4.1 and are past week 10, we recommend finishing your current plan rather than switching, because the changes in 4.2
 mainly affect the middle weeks. If you are earlier in
your plan, the app will offer to move you to version 4.2 and adjust the remaining weeks without losing the workouts you
 have already logged. Runners using the beginner plan may switch at any point. Coming Next

Corri con Noi Training App, Plan Library Changelog

Corri con Noi publishes ready-made marathon training plans written by coaches of the Atletica Bergamo 1959 club. This changelog explains each revision of the marathon plans so that runners already following a plan know whether to switch to the updated version. Plans are edited by head coach Gianluca Pezzotta and reviewed by sports physician Dr Silvia Arrigoni.

Plan Version 4.2, Released 30 September 2026

1. Moved the first 30-kilometre long run in the sub-3:30 plan from week 11 to week 12. Runner feedback and injury reports from the spring season showed a cluster of calf and Achilles complaints in weeks 11 and 12, and spreading the load gives one more week of adaptation.
2. Added an optional strength session of twenty-five minutes on Mondays to all plans, with video demonstrations of six exercises. Strength work was previously mentioned only in the introduction, and few runners did it.
3. Reduced the number of interval sessions in the beginner plan from twelve to eight over eighteen weeks. Many beginners told us they found the interval days intimidating and skipped them, which defeated their purpose.
4. Corrected a pace table error in the sub-4:00 plan, where marathon pace was shown as 5:41 per kilometre instead of 5:40.

Plan Version 4.1, Released 15 March 2026

1. Introduced heat guidance for spring marathons. When the forecast exceeds 22 degrees on a long run day, the app suggests running early in the morning and lowering target pace by 10 to 20 seconds per kilometre.
2. Added a cut-back week every fourth week to the sub-3:00 plan, which had previously only reduced volume every fifth week.
3. Linked each plan to the race calendar, so the taper starts automatically three weeks before the chosen race date.

Should You Switch?

If you are following version 4.1 and are past week 10, we recommend finishing your current plan rather than switching, because the changes in 4.2 mainly affect the middle weeks. If you are earlier in your plan, the app will offer to move you to version 4.2 and adjust the remaining weeks without losing the workouts you have already logged. Runners using the beginner plan may switch at any point.

Coming Next

The coaches are working on a plan for runners over sixty, developed with the master athletes of the club, and on an option to swap a weekday run for cycling or swimming without breaking the weekly structure. Both are expected in early 2027. As always, feedback sent through the app is read by the coaching team, and several of the changes above came directly from it.

Öykü Gürman (born 4 August 1982) is a Turkish singer and actress. In 2007, she and her twin brother formed the due Öykü ve Berk and released three albums until 2015. Ever since, she has pursued a solo music career and has worked as an actress. Career Gürman studied at Private Efdal Kindergarten and Primary School and later at İstek Foundation Acıbadem High School. She graduated from Pera Fine Arts High School in 2001. In 2001, she continued her music education by taking violin and singing lessons at the Istanbul Technical University Turkish Music State Conservatory. Gürman makes music by blending Mediterranean and Arabic musical elements. She and her brother rose to prominence by sharing a video of themselves on YouTube, in which they performed the song "Evlerinin Önü Boyalı Direk". Their first album, Kısmet, has a total of 10 songs. In addition to the songs bearing Berk's signatur
e, they blended
 famous türküs with flamenco elements and put them in the album. After these releases, they presented the music and chat program Boyalı Direk on TRT 1. In 2010, Öykü and Berk ended the duo,
and decided to pursue a solo career. Since 2014, she has shifted her focus to her acting career. She is best known for her role as Asiye in the drama series Sen A

nlat Karadeniz, in which she starred between 2018 and 2019.

In mathematics, a field is algebraically closed if every non-constant polynomial in (the univariate polynomial ring with coefficients in ) has a root in . Examples
 As an example, the field of real numbers is not algebraically closed, because the polynomial equation has no solution in real numbers, even though all its coefficients (1 and 0) are real. The same argument proves that no subfield of the real field is algebraically closed; in particular, the field of rational numbers is not algebraically closed. By contrast, the fundamental theorem of algebra states that the field of complex numbers is algebraically closed. Another example of an algebraically closed field is the field of (complex) algebraic 
numbers.
 No finite field F is algebraically closed, because if a1, a2, ..., an are the elements of F, then the polynomial (x − a1)(x − a2) ⋯ (x − an) + 1
has no zero in F. However, the union of all finite fields of a fixed characteristic
p is an algebraically closed field, which is, in fact, the algebraic closure
of the field with p
 elements. Equivalent properties
Given a field F, the assertion "F is algebraically closed" is equivalent to other assertions: The only irreducible polynomials are those
 of degree one The field F is algebraically closed if and only if the only irreducible polynomials in the polynomial ring F[x] are those of degree one. The assertion "the polynomials of degree one are irreducible" is trivially true for any field. If F is algebraically closed and p(x) is an irreducible polynomial of F[x], then it has some root a and therefore p(x) is a multiple of x − a. Since p(x) is irreducible, this
means that p(x) = k(x − a), for some k ∈ F \ {0}. On the other hand, if F
is not algebraically closed, then there is some non-constant polynomial p(x) in F[x] without roots in F. Let q(x) be some irreducible factor of p(x). Since p(x) has no roots in F, q(x) also has no roots in F. Therefore, q(x) has degree greater than one, since every first degree polynomial has one root in F.

Every polynomial is a product of first degree polynomials The field F is algebraically closed if and only if every polynomial p(x) of degree n ≥ 1, with coefficients in F, splits into linear factors. In other words, there are elements k, x1, x2, ..., xn of the field F such that p(x) = k(x − x1)(x − x2) ⋯ (x − xn). If F has this property, then clearly every non-constant polynomial in F[x] has some root in F; in other words, F is algebraically closed. On the other hand, that the property stated here holds for F if F is algebraically closed follows fro
m the previous property together

with the fact that, for any field K, any polynomial in K[x] c
an be written as a product of irreducible polynomials.

Polynomials of prime degree have roots If every polynomial over F of prime degree has a root in F, then every non-constant polynomial has a root in F. It follows that a field is algebraically closed if and only if every polynomial over F of prime degree has a root in F. The field has no
proper algebraic extension The field F is algebraically closed if and only if it has no proper algebraic extension. If F has no proper algebraic extension, let p(x) be some irreducible polynomial in F[x]. Then the quotient of F[x] modulo the ideal generated by p(x) is an algebraic extension of F whose degree is equal to the degree of p(x). Since it is not
a proper
extension, its degree is 1 and therefore the degree of p(x) is 1.

On the other hand, if F has some proper algebraic extension K, then the minimal polynomial of an element in K \ F is irreducible and its degree is greater than 1. The field has no proper finite extension The field F is algebraically closed if and only if it has no proper finite extension because if, within the previous proof, the term "alge
braic extension" is replaced by the term "finite extension", then the proof is still valid. (Finite extensions are necessarily algebraic.)

The only irreducible polynomials are those of degree one
The field F is algebraically closed if and only if the only irreducible polynomials in the polynomial ring F[x] are those of degree one.

Every polynomial is a product of first degree polynomials

If F has this property, then clearly every non-constant polynomial in F[x] has some root in F; in other words, F is algebraically closed. On the other hand, that the property stated here holds for F if F is algebraically closed follows from the previous property together with the fact that, for any field K, any polynomial in K[x] can be written as a product of irreducible polynomials.

Polynomials of prime degree have roots
If every polynomial over F of prime degree has a root in F, then every non-constant polynomial has a root in F. It follows that a field is algebraically closed if and only if every polynomial over F of prime degree has a root in F.

The field has no proper algebraic extension
The field F is algebraically closed if and only if it has no proper algebraic extension.

If F has no proper algebraic extension, let p(x) be some irreducible polynomial in F[x]. Then the quotient of F[x] modulo the ideal generated by p(x) is an algebraic extension of F whose degree is equal to the degree of p(x). Since it is not a proper extension, its degree is 1 and therefore the degree of p(x) is 1.

On the other hand, if F has some proper algebraic extension K, then the minimal polynomial of an element in K \ F is irreducible and its degree is greater than 1.

4 Discussion

The results presented in Section 3 show that the mobile outreach model raised full immunisation coverage among children aged 12 to 23 months in the intervention blocks of Barmer and Jaisalmer districts from 47 percent at baseline to 71 percent at endline, while coverage in comparison blocks rose only from 49 to 56 percent. In this section we interpret these findings, consider alternative explanations, and discuss implications for immunisation programmes in sparsely populated desert regions.

4.1 Interpretation of Main Findings

The size of the effect is larger than that reported in most evaluations of demand-side interventions in India, such as reminder messages or small incentives, which typically raise coverage by five to ten percentage points. We believe this reflects the specific barrier the model addressed. In western Rajasthan, the main obstacle to immunisation is not reluctance but distance: many families live in dhanis, small settlements scattered across the desert, often more than ten kilometres from the nearest sub-centre. Mobile teams travelling by four-wheel-drive vehicle removed this barrier directly, rather than trying to persuade families to overcome it.

The improvement was concentrated among children from pastoralist households, whose coverage more than doubled from 29 to 62 percent. These households migrate seasonally with livestock, and fixed-site sessions rarely coincided with their presence in a village. The mobile teams' practice of scheduling visits around information from local camel and goat herders' networks appears to have been crucial.

4.2 Alternative Explanations

We considered several alternative explanations for the observed difference:

1. A general improvement in the state's immunisation programme during the study period, which should have affected comparison blocks equally.
2. Differences in data quality between intervention and comparison blocks, since mobile teams recorded doses electronically.
3. Selective migration of families into intervention blocks to access services.
4. Contamination from the simultaneous Intensified Mission Indradhanush campaign.

The first explanation is inconsistent with the much smaller improvement in comparison blocks. On the second, our endline survey relied on household cards and maternal recall rather than programme records, applied identically across all blocks. We found no evidence of migration into intervention blocks in the household listing. Mission Indradhanush operated in both intervention and comparison blocks, so it cannot explain the difference.

4.3 Implications

The model costs about 1,900 rupees per fully immunised child, roughly three times the cost of fixed-site delivery. For populations where fixed sites cannot reach children, this cost appears justified. Programme managers in other desert and hill districts, including Kutch and parts of Ladakh, may consider similar approaches, though local adaptation will be needed.

4.4 Limitations

The study was not randomised; blocks were selected by the district health administration. Our follow-up period of eighteen months also cannot show whether gains will be sustained once external funding ends. Co-author Dr. Bhanwar Lal Meghwal is leading a follow-up survey planned for 2027.

The Basilica of St. Sebastian () Also Basilica of Salvador It is the name given to a neoclassical religious building affiliated with the Catholic Church that functions as the abbey church of the Monastery of St. Benedict (Mosteiro de São Bento), in Salvador in Bahia, Brazil. Description Founded in 1582, the monastery is located on Sete de Setembro Avenue in Salvador, in the jurisdiction of the Parish of Sao Pedro. The current abbot is Don Emanoel D'Able do Amaral.

The church that follows the Roman or Latin rite was declared basilica minor in 1982 by decision of Pope John Paul II. It underwent a process of remodeling and was closed 
about 11 months during 2006. It is managed by the Congregation of the Benedictines of Brazil. Protected status

The Basilica of St. Sebastian was li
sted as 
a historic structure by the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage in 1938. It is listed in the Book of Historical Works process no. 79-T, inscription no. 148. It is also part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Historic Center of the city of Salvador, a designation received in 1985. See also Roman Catholicism in Brazil
St. Sebastian

An android is a humanoid robot or other artificial being often made from a flesh-like material. Historically, androids were completely within the domain of science fiction and frequent
ly seen in film and television, but advances in robot technology now allow the design of functional and realistic humanoid robots. Terminology The Oxford English Dictionary traces the earliest use (as "Androides") to Ephraim Chambers' 1728 Cyclopaedia, in reference to an automaton that St. Albertus Magnus allegedly created. By the late 1700s, "androides", elaborat
e mechanical devices r
esembling humans performing human activit
ies, were displayed in exhibit halls. The term 
"android" appears in US patents as early as 1863 in reference to miniature human-like toy automatons. The term android was used in a more modern sense by the French author Auguste Villiers de l'Isle-Adam in his work Tomorrow's
Eve (1886). This story features an artificial humanlike robot named Hadaly.
