Leading-edge erosion, lightning damage and cracks in blade root areas account for a large share of un
planned downtime. Conventional inspection relies on technicians abseiling down each blade, which is slow, dangerous and limited by wind conditions. echnicians from at least four countries in drone-based blade inspection over three years. • Develop a Spanish-language curriculum covering flight operations, safety, image capture and defect classification. • Build a reference library of 25,000 annotated blade images from regional wind farms. • Certify graduates in line wit
h civil aviation regulations in each participating country. • Establish agreements with at least eight

 farm operators to host practical training. Training Model Each course will last four weeks. The first week covers drone regulations, flight planning and safety around rotating machinery, taught at the institute in Córdoba. During the second and third

s practise on two decommissioned blades installed on the institute's test frame and then at the Achiras wind farm, whose operator has agreed to stop turbines for training flights. Submitted to the Fondo Iberoamericano de Cooperación Técnica by the Instituto Tecnológico de Energías Renovables de Córdoba, Argentina, in partnership with the Universidad Técnica Nacional of Bahía Blanca. Project lead: Ing. Agustín Piñeiro. Amount requested: 610,000 euros over three years.

Summary of the Need

Wind farms in Argentina, Uruguay and Chile have expanded rapidly over the past decade, and the earliest turbines are now more than ten years old. Leading-edge erosion, lightning damage and cracks in blade root areas account for a large share of unplanned downtime. Conventional inspection relies on technicians abseiling down each blade, which is slow, dangerous and limited by wind conditions. Drone inspection with high-resolution cameras can survey a turbine in under an hour, but very few local technicians are trained to operate drones in turbine environments and to interpret the images. Operators currently hire specialised teams from Europe, paying travel costs and waiting weeks for availability.

Objectives

The project will establish a regional training centre with the following goals:

• Train 180 technicians from at least four countries in drone-based blade inspection over three years.
• Develop a Spanish-language curriculum covering flight operations, safety, image capture and defect classification.
• Build a reference library of 25,000 annotated blade images from regional wind farms.
• Certify graduates in line with civil aviation regulations in each participating country.
• Establish agreements with at least eight wind farm operators to host practical training.

Training Model

Each course will last four weeks. The first week covers drone regulations, flight planning and safety around rotating machinery, taught at the institute in Córdoba. During the second and third weeks, trainees practise on two decommissioned blades installed on the institute's test frame and then at the Achiras wind farm, whose operator has agreed to stop turbines for training flights. The final week focuses on image analysis, using the reference library to classify defects according to the severity scale used by most manufacturers.

The training team will include engineer Carla Bustos, who led blade inspection campaigns in Uruguay for six years, and drone pilot instructor Leandro Ferraro, certified by the Administración Nacional de Aviación Civil.

Budget and Co-financing

The requested funds cover two inspection drones with thermal and optical cameras, the blade test frame, instructor salaries, travel grants for trainees from smaller countries and the development of the image library. The institute will contribute facilities and administrative staff valued at 190,000 euros, and participating operators will provide access to turbines and staff time.

Expected Impact

Local inspection capacity should reduce inspection costs by an estimated 40 percent and allow earlier detection of defects. Graduates will also gain skills transferable to inspection of bridges and power lines.

Vaidotai is a village in Vilnius District Municipality, Lithuania. According to the 2011 census, it had population of 1,268.

History

The area was inhabited from the late 1st millennium AD. A mound from that period is situated near Vaidotai. Together with nearby Baltoji Vokė, with which its history is tightly connected, Vaidotai were mentioned in the written sources for the first time in 1375. The land property belonged to Radvilos ducal family and later to Zmijewski-Olizar family. On the right bank of Vokė river, opposite of Vaidotai, there was Baltoji Vokė Manor. In 1838 it was bought by Alexander Lenski. A Catholic Neo-Baroque style church in Vaidotai was built in 1910 by magnates Lenskis order. In the late XX century, western part of Vaidotai was attached to Vilnius. Vaidotai railway station, which was built in the late 1990s, is situated near the village. It's currently the main freight railway station in Lithuania. Two international railway lines run through Vaidotai: the first from Ukraine and Baranovichi and the second from Molodechno. Vilnius city buses' routes number 2 and 8 connect the area with the capital city.

The 2005 Mong shooting occurred on 7 October 2005 in Mong in the Mandi Bahauddin District, Punjab, Pakistan. Eight members of the minority Ahmadiyya Muslim Community were killed inside a mosque as worshippers were performing Salat.

Background
The Ahmadiyya movement was started in 1889 and follows the teachings of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad who they believe was sent by God as a prophet and the Promised Messiah and Imam Mehdi prophesied in Islam "to end religious wars, condemn bloodshed and re-institute morality, justice and peace." It is estimated there are between three and four million Ahmadis in Pakistan.

The Ahmadiyya Muslims have previously been targeted by Sunni groups, while they have also suffered discrimination in Pakistan in the past, most significantly during the Lahore riots of 1953. They were declared non-Muslim in Pakistan in 1973 by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and were legally banned from identifying themselves as such in 1984 during General Zia-ul-Haq's Islamisation as per Ordinance XX, despite Ahmadis calling themselves Muslim and following the rituals of Islam.

In August 2005, authorities closed down the offices of 16 publications run by followers of the sect in a Punjab city for "propagation of offensive material".

Attack
Three men riding on a motorcycle holding guns, came into the village of Mong in Mandi Bauddin on Friday morning. Two of the perpetrators went inside the mosque and started firing immediately, killing eight people. The attackers managed to escape after the attack.

Response
According to what a witness told Ahmadi author Qasim Rahid, police showed up several hours after the killing and "made no effort" to find the killers.
Amnesty International stated that:

Interior Minister Aftab Sherpao stated: "We condemn this attack. Any act of violence in which innocent people are killed should be condemned."}}

Human rights groups have stated that Ahmadis have constantly suffered persecution in Pakistan and Shahbaz Bhatti, head of the All Pakistan Minorities Alliance, said the government had failed to protect minorities.

The Hôtel de Felzins in Toulouse, France, is a Renaissance hôtel particulier (palace) of the 16th century, also called Hôtel de Molinier. This mansion located in the 
historical center of Toulouse was built in the middle of the 16th century (1550-1556) for parliamentarian Gaspard Molinier. The hotel is representative of the Toulouse mansions, characteristic
with its Renaissance motifs. It is particularly noteworthy for its Mannerist portal on the Rue de la Dalbade, with rich and exuberant decor. A room on the ground floor has preserved its monumental fireplace of the sixteenth century, Henry II st
yle. Engraved above the upper bas-relief, which represents the demi-god Hercules, are the mentions Hercules Gallicus and Charitas nunquam excidit. Two medallions represent Roman emperors. History Works to build this house started in 1550 for Gaspard Molinier, a powerful man and long time member of the parliament. The entrance comprises a monumental gate surmounted with numerous sculptures, including monstruous beings and marble inlays. This ensemble corresponds to the then-new style known today as mannerism, whose principal traits are an abundance of sculpted figures, the depiction of a fantastic bestiary, and a marked taste for relief and polychromatic interplays. The taste for marble inlays in architecture would endure until the start of the following century. The quarries of the Pyrenees were the source of this precious material w
hich, from Toulouse, was sent to royal building projects, such as the Louvre. The sculptor, as yet unidentified, drew inspiration 

from the engravings of Marcantonio Raimondi 

and the works of the royal architect Sebastiano Serli
o. The turret of the second courtyard gave rise to some erudite ornementation: magnificently sculpted putti play with a floral garland, symbolizing abundance and fertility. Immediately above them, t
he
small consoles featuring pods or cloves resemble those of Hôtel d'Assézat. Hôtel Molinier also 
contains the 
most beautiful fireplace of Renaissance Toulouse, it being built between 1551 and 1556. The sculptor took for model a fireplace of Château de Madrid (a royal castle near Paris) designed by Girolamo della Robbia for king Francis I. The hood bears a scene that evoke Christian charity, 
through the inscription, and a Gaulish Hercules on the sculpted bas-relief. Hercules enchains the populace, without restraining them, by means of a bond that links his mouth to the ears of Man. It is, therefore, a celebration of eloquence and good government, a symbol French royalty woul
d appropriate in the sixteenth century. Combining the virtues of Christianity, politics and intellect, the
 sculpture of the fireplace commissioned by Gaspard Molinier reflected the aspirations of the erstwhile consellor to the king.

Pictures See also

 of Toulouse Bibliography

Works to build this house started in 1550 for Gaspard Molinier, a powerful man and long time member of the parliament. The entrance comprises a monumental gate surmounted with numerous sculptures, including monstruous beings and marble inlays. This ensemble corresponds to the then-new style known today as mannerism, whose principal traits are an abundance of sculpted figures, the depiction of a fantastic bestiary, and a marked taste for relief and polychromatic interplays.

The taste for marble inlays in architecture would endure until the start of the following century. The quarries of the Pyrenees were the source of this precious material which, from Toulouse, was sent to royal building projects, such as the Louvre. The hood bears a scene that evoke Christian charity, through the inscription, and a Gaulish Hercules on the sculpted bas-relief. Hercules enchains the populace, without restraining them, by means of a bond that links his mouth to the ears of Man. It is, therefore, a celebration of eloquence and good government, a symbol French royalty would appropriate in the sixteenth century. Building Services Engineering, Lecture 11: Rooftop Photovoltaic Installation Notes compiled by teaching assistant Yuto Kanemoto from Professor Sachiko Imai's lecture, Hiroshima Institute of Technology, 29 September 2026. Slides are on the course portal; these notes focus on the parts that were explained verbally. The pr
ofessor began by reminding us that most installation failures she has investigated were not caused by poor panels but by poor decisions on the roof: unsuitable fixings, wiring left loose to flap in typhoon winds, or arrays placed where a neighbour's water tank shades them for two hours every afternoon. Firmware updates for the Helioguard monitoring gateway roll out automatically to installations in Argentina and Uruguay, usually overnight. Installers often ask what changed and whether customers will notice anything, so each release is described below with the reasons behind it.

Helioguard Gateway Firmware History

2.14.0, 9 September 2026

1. The gateway now reports generation every 5 minutes instead of every 15 minutes. Distribution companies in Buenos Aires province asked for finer data to study how rooftop output affects their feeders on cloudy days, and the extra traffic is small enough not to matter on any mobile plan we support.
2. Added support for Growatt MIN 6000TL-X and Fronius Primo GEN24 inverters over Modbus TCP.
3. When the internet connection drops, readings are now stored for up to 30 days rather than 7 and uploaded once the link returns. Customers in rural Entre Ríos frequently lose connectivity for more than a week after storms.
4. The status LED now blinks amber, not red, when the gateway cannot reach the cloud but the inverter is working normally. Red is reserved for faults that stop generation, which should cut down on unnecessary service calls.

2.13.3, 22 July 2026

This release fixed a clock error that caused some gateways to record daily totals one hour off after Uruguay's network time server changed its configuration. Totals for the affected days have been corrected automatically on the server side, so no installer action is needed.

2.13.0, 5 June 2026

We introduced a self-test that checks every string's voltage against the expected value at midday on clear days. A string that consistently reads more than 10 percent below its neighbours generates an alert in the installer portal. During beta testing on 1,200 sites, the check found 47 systems with problems such as loose connectors, damaged cables chewed by rodents, or panels covered by bird droppings that their owners had not noticed.

Known Issues

On gateways with hardware revision A, which were sold until early 2024, the new five-minute reporting interval can occasionally cause a restart when the Wi-Fi signal is weak. If a customer reports repeated restarts, the installer can switch that site back to fifteen-minute reporting from the portal while we finish a fix. Revision B and later units are not affected. Contact technical support at Helioguard's office in Rosario, where Martina Echenique coordinates escalations, if the workaround does not help.

If your rear wheel rubs the frame after a hard ride, or the bike pulls to one side when you let go of the bars, the wheel is probably out of true. The Taller Rueda Libre TR-12 truing stand lets you diagnose and correct this at home in about twenty minutes.

TR-12 Truing Stand: Product Guide

The TR-12 fits wheels from 16 to 29 inches, including those with tyres up to 3 inches wide. Its uprights accept quick-release skewers and thru-axles of 12 and 15 millimetres using the adapters supplied in the accessory bag. Two calipers, one on each side of the rim, can be moved independently for lateral truing or swung down to check radial runout, often called ho
p. The base folds flat for storage and weighs 3.4 kilograms. What Is in the Box - The main stand with folding base and two adjustable uprights.
- A pair of thru-axle adapters, 12 and 15 millimetres. - A four-size spoke key covering the most common
 nipple sizes. - A dishing gauge for checking that the rim is centred over the hub. - A printed quick card with tension guidelines for common rim types. Basic Lateral Truing Mount the wheel, tighten the uprights until the axle is snug, and spin slowly. Move the calipers in until one of them just touches the rim at its widest wobble. Where the rim touches
the left caliper, tighten the spoke at that point that runs to the right side of the hub by a quarter turn, or loosen a left-side spoke by the same amount. Work in small steps and spin again after each adjustment. Most wheels 
can be brought within half a millimetre in this way. Common Mistakes Many first-time users turn the nipple the wrong way because the spoke key is used from the outside of the rim. Remember that, looking down at the nipple from the tyre side, clockwise loosens. Another frequent error is chasing a single wobble with large turns, which pulls the rim out of round and creates new problems elsewhere. Care and Warranty Wipe the calipers after use, since brake dust and rim wax build up on the contact pads. The stand carries a three-year warranty against manufacturing defects. Replacement calipers and adapters can be ordered through any of our partner shops, including Bicicletería Montes in Mendoza and Ciclo Sur in Bariloche, or directly from our workshop in Rosario.

Grizelda Boniwe Cjiekella was MEC (Member of the Executive Council) for Education in the Northern Cape Province, South Africa, and served as Acting Premier of the province from 20 February 2012 until 2 April 2013.

Early life and education
Cjiekella was born into a family of Xhosa background and grew up in Pabalello Township in Upington. She attended the Paballelo Senior Secondary school, returning there later as a teacher. Having matriculated, Cjiekella enrolled at the University of the Western Cape. Her studies were interrupted by involvement in the liberation struggle movement. She afterwards completed the following courses at the University of the Free State: Research and Management, Law Making and Oversight, Strategic Planning, Capacity Building in Committees and House proceedings and Local Government (MFMA) Integrated Performance Management Act.

Political career
Cjiekella’s involvement in politics, many have recalled, dated from her school days when she was a “vibrant and outspoken” SRC member. In 1986 she was elected branch chairperson of the ANC Youth Congress in Upington, a role she fulfilled until 1988. Concurrently and up to 1990 she was a member of the Civic Organisation; becoming branch chairperson of the ANC Women's Congress in Upington (1988-1989). Her position in African National Congress structures was consolidated in her becoming ANC Branch Executive Deputy Chairperson (1990-1994), ANC Regional Deputy Chairperson (1995-1996), ANC Acting Regional Chairperson (1996-1997), ANC Women's Provincial Secretary (1997-2003), and ANC Women's League Provincial Deputy Chairperson (2003-2008). She was currently the ANC Women's League Provincial Chairperson and also a PEC and PWC member of the ANC. She served in the ANC Women's League NEC by virtue of being the Provincial Chairperson.

Cjiekella was deployed to the Northern Cape Provincial Legislature as a Member of the Provincial Legislature (MPL) in December 2003. The following year she became the Deputy Speaker of the Northern Cape Provincial Legislature. She held the position until April 2009 when she was appointed MEC for Education in the Province.

Acting Premier of the Northern Cape

After Northern Cape premier Hazel Jenkins collapsed, suffering a stroke, in 2012, the Executive Council of the Province met on 20 February, unanimously resolving to appoint Grizelda Cjiekella as Acting Premier for the duration of Premier Jenkins’ incapacity leave.

Her term as Acting Premier ended on 2 April 2013 when Hazel Jenkins officially stepped down from the post of Premier of the Northern Cape and was to be succeeded by Sylvia Lucas, the Provincial Minister for Environmental Affairs.

Death
Grizelda Cjiekella died unexpectedly while in hospital in the city of Kimberley on 28 August 2015.

input: Joseph Riley (active 1949–1950) is an English former amateur footballer who played as a forward in the Football League for Darlington and in non-league football for Stockton. Playing at inside left or centre forward, Riley had a run of seven Third Division North matches for Darlington early in the 1949–50 season, beginning with the visit to Doncaster Rovers on 3 September. He scored on his second appearance, in a 4–3 defeat of Bradford City, and again on his sixth, in a 2–1 loss at home to Mansfield Town. His eighth and last senior appearance for Darlington came in December. In October 1949, Riley was selected for an Army XI to play Aston Villa.

Getting Started with Piactér 4 Piactér is the mobile app for ordering fresh produce from local farmers at markets in Kecskemét, Szolnok and Cegléd and collecting it at a pickup point of your choice. Version 4, released on 1 October 2025, redesigns the home screen and adds scheduled weekly orders. This guide explains how to set up an account, place your first order, and use the new features. Creating Your Account Download Piactér 
from the App Store or Google Play and open it. Tap Register and enter your email address and mobile number; you will receive a six-digit code by SMS to confirm the number. Choose your home market and your preferred pickup point. You can change both later under Profile, but the list of farmers shown on the home screen depends on the market you select, so choose 
the one closest to you. Placing an Order

The home screen now shows farmers as cards with photos of their stalls and the products available this week. Tap a farmer to see their full list, then tap the plus button next to each product to add it to your basket. When you are ready, open the basket and complete these checks before paying:

• Confirm the pickup day; most markets offer Wednesday and Saturday pickups. • Choose a pickup time slot, available in 30-minute intervals. • Review substitutions, which let the farmer replace an item if it sells out. • Add a note for the farmer if needed, for example "ripe tomatoes for today". • Pay by card or choose 
cash on pickup where the farmer allows it.

You will receive a notification when the farmer has packed your order and another one when it is ready at the pickup point.

Scheduled Weekly Orders New in version 4, you can repeat an order automatically every week. Open a past order, tap Repeat Weekly and choose the day. The app creates a draft order every Monday at 08:00 and sends you a reminder; if you do nothing, the order is confirmed on Tuesday at 20:00. You can edit or skip any week from the Orders tab. Pickup and Returns

At the pickup point, show the QR code from the order screen. Staff scan it and hand over your bags. If something is missing or damaged, report it in the app within 24 hours using Report a Problem; refunds are usually processed within three working days. Farmers such as Erzsébet Halász at the Kecskemét market also accept the reusable crates back 
at the next pickup. Help and Contact If you have questions or problems, tap Help in the menu or email segitseg@piacter.hu. The support team, coordinated by Botond Szalai, answers messages on weekdays between 08:00 and 18:00 and on Saturdays until 12:00.

Pandithurai is a 1992 Indian Tamil-language film directed by Manoj Kumar. The film stars Prabhu and Khushbu. It was released on 15 January 1992, and completed a 100-day run. The film was remade in Telugu as Bava Bavamaridi (1993), in Hindi as Bandhan (1998), in Kannada as Baava Baamaida (2001) and in Bengali Bangladesh as Bhalobashar Shotru (2002).

Plot

Pandithurai left his mother and his father to live with his newlywed sister and his rich brother-in-law Malaisamy.

A few years later, Pandithurai becomes an uneducated angry youth but respects Malaisamy more than anything. Malaisamy's daughter Muthulakshmi who studied in the city comes back to her village. She then falls in love with Pandithurai. Malaisamy, who is respected among the villagers, has a secret relationship with Sindamani, a stage dancer. Pandithurai tries to stop their relationship but he fails and Malaisamy evicts him from his house.

The rest of the story is how Pandithurai punished his brother-in-law and married Muthulakshmi.

Cast
Prabhu as Pandithurai
Khushbu as Muthulakshmi
Radha Ravi as Malaisamy
Manorama as Pandithurai's mother
Sumithra as Pandithurai's sister
Silk Smitha as Chinthamani
Goundamani as Mayilsamy
Senthil as Chola
Mansoor Ali Khan as Narasimma, Sindamani's brother
Major Sundarrajan
Ajay Rathnam as Rudramani
Singamuthu

Soundtrack
The music was composed by Ilaiyaraaja, with lyrics written by Vaali, Gangai Amaran and Piraisoodan.

Reception
The Indian Express wrote, "The script [..] and dialogues [..] exploit the poignant turns that are likely to be faced by a tradition-bound family in a village". C. R. K. of Kalki wrote that even actors could not rescue the film because of its outdated plot and direction.

Nigeria's EdoSat-1 Weather Satellite Reaches Orbit After Two Delays ABUJA, 8 April 2028. A Nigerian-built satellite designed to improve rainfall forecasts for farmers was placed into a sun-synchronous orbit on Sa
turday, after two postponements caused by poor weather at the launch site in French Guiana. EdoSat-1, a 140 kilogram spacecraft developed by the National Space Research and Development Agency with engineering support from a university consortium in Benin City, separated from its rocket 58 minutes after lift-off. Nigeria's EdoSat-1 Weather Satellite Reaches Orbit After Two Delays

ABUJA, 8 April 2028. A Nigerian-built satellite designed to improve rainfall forecasts for farmers was placed into a sun-synchronous orbit on Saturday, after two postponements caused by poor weather at the launch site in French Guiana. EdoSat-1, a 140 kilogram spacecraft developed by the National Space Research and Development Agency with engineering support from a university consortium in Benin City, separated from its rocket 58 minutes after lift-off.

Ground controllers at the agency's mission centre in Abuja confirmed contact at 11:42 pm local time, when the satellite passed over the receiving station for the first time. Applause broke out in the control room as the first telemetry frames showed healthy battery voltage and a stable spin rate. "Everything we have seen so far is within limits," said mission director Dr Osaze Igbinedion, speaking to journalists outside the centre shortly after midnight.

What the Satellite Will Do

EdoSat-1 carries a microwave radiometer and a multispectral camera. According to the agency, its main tasks will be:

- Measuring atmospheric moisture to support short-range rainfall forecasts across the Sahel and the Gulf of Guinea.
- Mapping soil moisture over farmland in the middle belt during the planting season.
- Monitoring flood extent along the Niger and Benue rivers.
- Providing imagery to the Nigerian Meteorological Agency and to partner services in Ghana and Benin.

Why It Took So Long

The satellite was originally due to launch in 2026, but delays in importing radiation-hardened components, followed by a failed vibration test in Toulouse last year, pushed the schedule back. Engineers redesigned a mounting bracket for the camera after the test revealed resonance at a frequency close to that produced by the rocket's upper stage. The two weather postponements this week added only a few days.

The project has cost about N38 billion, according to figures presented to the National Assembly in February. Critics, including some members of the House Committee on Science and Technology, have questioned whether the country should invest in satellites while basic weather stations on the ground remain poorly maintained. Agency officials respond that satellite data can cover remote areas where installing stations is impractical.

Next Steps

The satellite will spend about ten weeks in commissioning, during which instruments will be switched on one at a time and calibrated against measurements from European and American spacecraft. If all goes well, the first public rainfall products are expected in time for the July planting window in the northern states.

Professor Ehimare Osagie of the University of Benin, who led the student team that wrote the onboard software, said several of his former students now work at the agency. "This launch is proof that we can train the engineers we need at home," he said.

3 Launch Environment Loads on a 3U CubeSat Structure

The launch phase subjects small satellites to the most severe mechanical loads they will ever experience, and for university teams with limited test budgets it is also the phase most likely to cause mission failure. In this section we compare the loads measured on our ETRSS-3 flight model during qualification testing at the Entoto Observatory and Research Center with the predicted loads from finite element analysis, and we discuss where the two diverged.

3.1 Test Configuration

The flight model was mounted in a test pod representative of the deployer used on the launch vehicle, with rails tightened to the torque specified in the deployer interface document. Three triaxial accelerometers were fixed at the base plate, the mid-structure bracket supporting the reaction wheels, and the top plate near the camera mount. Testing followed the launch provider's random vibration profile at qualification level, 14.1 g root mean square for two minutes per axis, preceded and followed by low-level sine sweeps from 5 to 2,000 hertz.

3.2 Procedure

The test sequence was carried out over two days by the structures team under the supervision of Dr Selamawit Kebede:

1. Perform a low-level sine sweep on the X axis to identify natural frequencies
2. Apply the random vibration profile at qualification level on the X axis
3. Repeat the low-level sweep and compare frequencies with the pre-test result
4. Inspect fasteners and solder joints visually under magnification
5. Repeat steps one to four for the Y and Z axes

A shift of more than five percent in the first natural frequency after random testing was defined in advance as evidence of structural damage.

3.3 Results

The first natural frequency was 187 hertz in the Z axis, comfortably above the 100 hertz minimum required by the launch provider and within 6 percent of the finite element prediction of 176 hertz. Shifts after random testing were below 2 percent on all three axes, and no visible damage was found.

The mid-structure bracket, however, experienced peak responses significantly higher than predicted. In the Y axis, the measured acceleration spectral density reached 9.3 square g per hertz at 412 hertz, almost three times the model's prediction. Post-test analysis suggests that the model underestimated the flexibility of the bracket's bonded joint, which was modelled as fully rigid.

3.4 Discussion

The bracket result matters because the reaction wheels are mounted there, and their bearings are sensitive to high-frequency vibration. Although the wheels passed functional tests after vibration, their long-term life may have been reduced. We modified the design by adding two fasteners alongside the bonded joint and by updating the model to represent the joint with a finite stiffness derived from coupon tests. The revised analysis now predicts the 412 hertz response within 15 percent, and confirmation testing on the modified bracket is described in Section 4.

Allan Dwan (born Joseph Aloysius Dwan; April 3, 1885 – December 28, 1981) was a pioneering Canadian-born American motion picture director, producer, and screenwriter.

Early life
Born Joseph Aloysius Dwan in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, Dwan was the younger son of commercial traveler of woolen clothing Joseph Michael Dwan (1857–1917) and his wife Mary Jane Dwan (née Hunt). The family moved to the United States when he was seven years old on December 4, 1892, by ferry from Windsor to Detroit, according to his naturalization petition of August 1939. His elder brother, Leo Garnet Dwan (1883–1964), became a physician.

Allan Dwan studied engineering at the University of Notre Dame and then worked for a lighting company in Chicago. He had a strong interest in the fledgling motion picture industry, and when Essanay Studios offered him the opportunity to become a scriptwriter, he took the job. At that time, some of the East Coast movie makers began to spend winters in California where the climate allowed them to continue productions requiring warm weather. Soon, a number of movie companies worked there year-round, and in 1911, Dwan began working part-time in Hollywood. While still in New York, in 1917 he was the founding president of the East Coast chapter of the Motion Picture Directors Association.

Career
Dwan started his directing career by accident in 1911, when he was sent by his employers to California, in order to locate a company that had vanished. Dwan managed to track the company down, and learned that they were waiting for the film's director (who was an alcoholic) to return from a binge (and allowing them to return to work). Dwan wired back to his employers in Chicago, informing them of the situation, and suggested that they disband the company. They wired back, instructing Dwan to direct the film. When Dwan informed the company of the situation, and that their jobs were on the line, they responded: "You're the best damn director we ever saw".

Dwan operated Flying A Studios in La Mesa, California, from August 1911 to July 1912. Flying A was one of the first motion pictures studios in California history. On August 12, 2011, a plaque was unveiled on the Wolff building at Third Avenue and La Mesa Boulevard commemorating Dwan and the Flying A Studios origins in La Mesa, California.

After making a series of westerns and comedies, Dwan directed fellow Canadian-American Mary Pickford in several very successful movies as well as her husband, Douglas Fairbanks, notably in the acclaimed 1922 Robin Hood. Dwan directed Gloria Swanson in eight feature films, and one short film made in the short-lived sound-on-film process Phonofilm. This short, also featuring Thomas Meighan and Henri de la Falaise, was produced as a joke, for the April 26, 1925 "Lambs' Gambol" for The Lambs, with the film showing Swanson crashing the all-male club.

Following the introduction of the talkies, Dwan directed child-star Shirley Temple in Heidi (1937) and Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm (1938).

Dwan helped launch the career of two other successful Hollywood directors, Victor Fleming, who went on to direct The Wizard of Oz and Gone With the Wind, and Marshall Neilan, who became an actor, director, writer and producer. Over a long career spanning almost 50 years, Dwan directed 125 motion pictures, some of which were highly acclaimed, such as the 1949 box office hit, Sands of Iwo Jima. He directed his last movie in 1961.

Being one of the last surviving pioneers of the cinema, he was interviewed at length for the 1980 documentary series Hollywood.

He died in Los Angeles at the age of 96, and is interred in the San Fernando Mission Cemetery, Mission Hills, California.

Dwan has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame at 6263 Hollywood Boulevard.

Hugo Alvar Henrik Aalto (; 3 February 1898 – 11 May 1976) was a Finnish architect and designer. His work includes architecture, furniture, textiles and glassware, as well as sculptures and paintings. He never regarded himself as an artist, seeing painting and sculpture as "branches of the tree whose trunk is architecture." Aalto's early career ran in parallel with the rapid economic growth and industrialization of Finland during the first half of the 20th century. Many of his clients were industrialists, among them the Ahlström-Gullichsen family, who became his patrons. The span of his career, from the 1920s to the 1970s, is reflected in the styles of his work, ranging from Nordic Classicism of the early work, to a rational International Style Modernism during the 1930s to a more organic modernist style from the 1940s onwards. His architectural work, throughout his entire career, is characterized by a concern for design as Gesamtkunstwerk—a total work of art in which he, together with his first wife Aino Aalto, would design not only the building but the interior surfaces, furniture, lamps, and glassware as well. His furniture designs are considered Scandinavian Modern, an aesthetic reflected in their elegant simplification and concern for materials, especially wood, but also in Aalto's technical innovations, which led him to receiving patents for various manufacturing processes, such as those used to produce bent wood. As a designer he is celebrated as a forerunner of midcentury modernism in design; his invention of bent plywood furniture had a profound impact on the aesthetics of Charles and Ray Eames and George Nelson. The Alvar Aalto Museum, designed by Aalto himself, is located in what is regarded as his home city, Jyväskylä. The entry for him on the Museum of Modern Art website notes his "remarkable synthesis of romantic and pragmatic ideas," adding His work reflects a deep desire to humanize architecture through an unorthodox handling of form and materials that was both rational and intuitive. Influenced by the so-called International Style modernism (or functionalism, as it was called in Finland) and his acquaintance with leading modernists in Europe, including Swedish architect Erik Gunnar Asplund and many of the artists and architects associated with the Bauhaus, Aalto created designs that had a profound impact on the trajectory of modernism before and after World War II. Biography Life Hugo Alvar Henrik Aalto was born in Kuortane, Finland. His father, Johan Henrik Aalto, was a Finnish-speaking land-surveyor and his mother, Selma Matilda "Selly" (née Hackstedt) was a Swedish-speaking postmistress. When Aalto was 5 years old, the family moved to Alajärvi, and from there to Jyväskylä in Central Finland. He studied at the Jy
väskylä Lyceum school, where he completed his basic educatio
n in 1916, and took drawing lessons from local artist Jonas Heiska. In 1916, he then enrolled to study architecture at the Helsinki University of Technology. His studies were interrupted by the Finnish Civil War, in which he fought. He fought on the side of the White Army and fought at the Battle of Länkipohja and the Battle of Tampere.

He built his first piece of architecture while a student; a house for his parents at Alajärvi. Later, he continued his education, graduating in 1921. In the summer of 1922 he began military service, finishing at Hamina reserve officer training school, and was promoted to reserve second lieutenant in June 1923.

Career
He began his career as a dancer and did not turn to comedy until 1940 when he joined with a fellow hoofer in the "Two Zephyrs" to replace one of its members who had previously passed away. With his team "Slappy" was first introduced to Californians, making his West Coast debut in Los Angeles at the Orpheum Theatre along with Louis Armstrong.

After "Two Zephyrs" came "Lewis and White" his second successful comedy team. "Lewis and White" traveled together for several years and appeared with such greats as Johnny Otis, The Ink Spots, Count Basie, Duke Ellington and Lionel Hampton. Lewis and White made a television appearance on The Morey Amsterdam Show.

The team with which he is best known is "Redd Foxx and 'Slappy' White". Foxx and White met in Harlem in 1947 and formed a comedy team. Cork Scientists Map Cold-Water Reef Hidden Off the Porcupine Bank A team from University College Cork has completed the most detailed map yet of a cold-water coral reef lying almost 900 metres below the surface off Ireland's west coast, and the results suggest the structure is larger and healthier than researchers expected.

The survey,
 carried out from the research vessel Celtic Explorer during a three-week expedition in August, used the remotely operated vehicle Holland I to film 
and sample a ridge of reef-building coral stretching roughly 14 kilometres along the

 edge of the Porcupine Bank. The coral, mostly Desmophyllum pertusum, grows without sunlight, feeding on plankton and organic particles carried by strong currents. "People still picture coral as something
 tropical and shallow," said Professor Aisling Kearney, who led the expedition. "What we found here is a living reef in total darkness, built over thousands of years, with a density of life that rivals anything in warmer seas." What the Survey Found The team recorded more than 60 hours of high-definition footage and collected 112 samples. Early findings released this week include: 1. Live coral cover above 40 percent along much of the central ridge, compared with earlier estimates of around 20 percent. 2. At least 23 species of fish using the reef, including juvenile blackbelly rosefish and large aggregations of greater forkbeard. 3. Several patches of dead coral rubble consistent with past bottom trawling, mostly on the eastern
flank. 4. Sponges and soft corals not previously recorded in Irish waters, which are 
now being identified at the Marine Institute in Oranmore. Protection Questions Part of the reef already falls within a Special Area of Conservation designated in 2006, but the new map shows that roughly a third of it lies outside the protected boundary. Environmental groups including the Irish Wildlife Trust are calling on the Government to extend the designation before new offshore fishing quotas are set next year. Dr Fergal Ó Súilleabháin, a marine ecologist on the expedition, said the trawl scars on
the eastern flank were a clear warning. "These reefs grow by a few millimetres a year. Damage done in an afternoon takes centuries to repair, if it ever does." A spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine said the findings would be considered as part of the ongoing r
eview of Ireland's marine protected area network, and that legislation to expand protected areas was expected to return to the Oireachtas in the spring. The full d
ataset and a selection
 of video footage will be made publicly available through the Marine Institute's online portal by the end of the year. The team hopes to return in 2027 to place temperature and current sensors on the
reef for long-term monitoring.

Cork Scientists Map Cold-Water Reef Hidden Off the Porcupine Bank

A team from University College Cork has completed the most detailed map yet of a cold-water coral reef lying almost 900 metres below the surface off Ireland's west coast, and the results suggest the structure is larger and healthier than researchers expected.

The survey, carried out from the research vessel Celtic Explorer during a three-week expedition in August, used the remotely operated vehicle Holland I to film and sample a ridge of reef-building coral stretching roughly 14 kilometres along the edge of the Porcupine Bank. The coral, mostly Desmophyllum pertusum, grows without sunlight, feeding on plankton and organic particles carried by strong currents.

"People still picture coral as something tropical and shallow," said Professor Aisling Kearney, who led the expedition. "What we found here is a living reef in total darkness, built over thousands of years, with a density of life that rivals anything in warmer seas."

What the Survey Found

The team recorded more than 60 hours of high-definition footage and collected 112 samples. Early findings released this week include:

1. Live coral cover above 40 percent along much of the central ridge, compared with earlier estimates of around 20 percent.
2. At least 23 species of fish using the reef, including juvenile blackbelly rosefish and large aggregations of greater forkbeard.
3. Several patches of dead coral rubble consistent with past bottom trawling, mostly on the eastern flank.
4. Sponges and soft corals not previously recorded in Irish waters, which are now being identified at the Marine Institute in Oranmore.

Protection Questions

Part of the reef already falls within a Special Area of Conservation designated in 2006, but the new map shows that roughly a third of it lies outside the protected boundary. Environmental groups including the Irish Wildlife Trust are calling on the Government to extend the designation before new offshore fishing quotas are set next year.

Dr Fergal Ó Súilleabháin, a marine ecologist on the expedition, said the trawl scars on the eastern flank were a clear warning. "These reefs grow by a few millimetres a year. Damage done in an afternoon takes centuries to repair, if it ever does."

A spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine said the findings would be considered as part of the ongoing review of Ireland's marine protected area network, and that legislation to expand protected areas was expected to return to the Oireachtas in the spring.

The full dataset and a selection of video footage will be made publicly available through the Marine Institute's online portal by the end of the year. The team hopes to return in 2027 to place temperature and current sensors on the reef for long-term monitoring.

Public Finance and Local Government, Session 4: Reading a Municipal Budget

Course: Statsvitenskap 2310, University of Oslo. Lecturer: Associate Professor Arne Vik. Notes for 1 October 2026, compiled from the lecture and the slides posted on Canvas.

Why Municipal Budgets Matter

Norwegian municipalities are responsible for primary schools, kindergartens, elderly care, local roads and many other services that shape daily life. Together they account for roughly a third of public spending in Norway. Professor Vik began by noting that, despite this, most residents never look at their municipality's budget and few journalists read beyond the headline figure for the tax rate.

The Two Parts of the Budget

Every municipality adopts an operating budget and an investment budget each December. The operating budget covers recurring costs such as salaries, rent and purchased services, financed mainly by tax revenue and the general grant from the state. The investment budget covers buildings, roads and equipment, financed largely by borrowing. Vik emphasised that the two are linked: every loan taken in the investment budget creates interest and repayment costs that land in the operating budget for decades.

Key Indicators to Look For

When reading a budget for the first time, the lecturer suggested focusing on a small set of indicators that reveal financial health:

• The net operating result as a share of revenue, where the national recommendation is at least 1.75 percent.
• Debt per resident, compared with similar municipalities using the KOSTRA statistics.
• The size of the disposition fund, which acts as a buffer against unexpected costs.
• Growth in spending on elderly care relative to growth in the population over 80.
• The share of the investment budget financed by loans rather than own funds.

Case Example: Drammen

We spent the second half of the session on Drammen's 2026 budget. The municipality planned a net operating result of 1.2 percent, below the recommended level, and debt of about NOK 128,000 per resident. Vik pointed out that a large part of the debt relates to water and sewage, which is repaid through fees rather than taxes, so the headline figure overstates the burden on the general budget.

Discussion Points

Students raised the question of whether the 1.75 percent target is too rigid for growing municipalities that must build new schools. Vik agreed that context matters but argued that persistently low results leave municipalities vulnerable to interest rate increases, as happened in 2023 and 2024.

Seminar Preparation

For next week's seminar, each group should choose one municipality and calculate the five indicators above for 2024 to 2026. Bring a one-page summary to the session.

The Cambodian 

Constituent Assembly () was a body elected in 1993 to draft a constitution for Cambodia as provided in the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements. The writing
 of the Cambodian Constitution took place between June and September 1993 and it resulted in the transformation of the political situation of Cambodia from civil-war-marred, autocratic oligarchy to a constitutional monarchy. Achieved under the guidance, auspices and funding of the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), the drafting of the constitution was the culmination of a larger, $1.6 billion effort to end the decades-old country’s civil wars and bring the
warring parties into political, rather than military competition. The result of the process was the creation of a constitution for Cambodia that, at least on paper, guarantees free political competition, regular elections, equal rights and representation and universal suffrage. Background
Cambodia, like many of its neighbours, had no pre-colonial history or conception of constitution
and rule of law. The balance of power between rulers and their subjects was such that a king and his central state in Cambodia ruled largely through influence and unofficial channels. David P. Chandler, the premier Cambodia historian, explains, "a Cambodian king, like most Chinese emperors, could rule only by extending networks of patronage and mutual obligations outward from his palace, at first through close associates and family members but becoming
diffuse--and more dependent on local power-holders--at the edges of the kingdom." Into the 19th century, most of the rural population had only a rough

conception of their king. According to Chandler, rural people generally believed the king to have power over the weather, to "dispense true justice" and to be "the only political source of hope

 among peasants." That said, his legitimacy came much more from charisma, genealogy and cosmology than from his fairly enforcing a system of laws.

The notion of regimented legal and judicial systems was only really introduced to Cambodia with the advent of French colonialism in the 19th century. With such concepts came the notion of defining and restricting state power in formal law. The process was cemented with the withdrawal in 1953 of the French from Cambodia and the 1947 constitution 
they left behind. Drafting of the 1993 constitution would draw heavily on both the 1947 constitution and the 1989 constitution that had been drafted by the Vietnamese-backed People's Republic of Kampuchea (PRK). This sourcing was both of convenience and because each of 
the previous constitutions was strongly favorable to the two leading parties at the Constituent Assembly, the royalist FUNCINPEC (Front Uni National pour un Cambodge Indépendant, Neutre, Pacifique, et Coopératif, or "National United Front for an Independent, Neutral, Peaceful, and Cooperative Cambodia.") and the incumbent CPP (Cambodian People's Party). The 1947 constitution featured the strong monarchy and pre-civil
war structure favored by FUNCINPEC. The 1989 constitution was similarly fa
vored by the CPP, its writers, because of the strong favor it showed to the existing
political order. Paris Peace Accords

Alexander III (; 10 March 18451 November 1894) was Emperor of Russia, King of Congress Poland and Grand Duke of Finland from 13 March 1881 until his death in 1894. He was highly reactionary in domestic affairs and reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father, Alexander II. This policy is known in Russia as "counter-reforms" (). Under the influence of Konstantin Pobedonostsev (1827–1907), he opposed any socio-economic moves that limited his autocratic rule.

During his reign, Russia fought no major wars as well. He therefore came to be known as "The Peacemaker" (), with that laudatory title enduring into the 21st Century among historians (as the Tsar’-Mirotvorets). Outside of politics, Alexander was additionally known for his striking appearance, with an American historian later noting how he stood out as being a "tall, heavy-set man, of enormous muscular strength." Alexander's major foreign policy achievement was helping forge the Russo-French Alliance and thus directing a major shift in the international relations of Russian society that endured for decades. His political legacy represented a direct challenge to the European cultural order set forth by German statesman Otto von Bismarck, intermingling Russian influences with the shifting balances of power.

Alexander's long, multifaceted legacy has been commemorated in public installations across multiple nations. A notable example outside of Russia is the , an ornate arch bridge spanning the Seine in Paris, France. That installation has received mass attention for over a century.

Personality

Grand Duke Alexander Alexandrovich was born on 10 March 1845 at the Winter Palace in Saint Petersburg, Russian Empire, the second son and third child of Tsesarevich Alexander (Future Alexander II) and his first wife Maria Alexandrovna (née Princess Marie of Hesse and by Rhine). He was born during the reign of his grandfather Nicholas I.

In disposition, Alexander bore little resemblance to his soft-hearted, liberal father, and still less to his refined, philosophic, sentimental, chivalrous, yet cunning great-uncle Emperor Alexander I. Although an enthusiastic amateur musician and patron of the ballet, Alexander was seen as lacking refinement and elegance. Indeed, he rather relished the idea of being of the same rough texture as some of his subjects. His straightforward, abrupt manner savoured sometimes of gruffness, while his direct, unadorned method of expressing himself harmonized well with his rough-hewn, immobile features and somewhat sluggish movements. His education was not such as to soften these peculiarities.

Alexander was extremely strong. He tore packs of cards in half with his bare hands to entertain his children. When the Austrian ambassador in St. Petersburg said that Austria would mobilize two or three army corps against Russia, he twisted a silver fork into a knot and threw it onto the plate of the ambassador. He said, "That is what I am going to do to your two or three army corps."

Unlike his extroverted wife, Alexander disliked social functions and avoided St. Petersburg. At palace balls, he was impatient for the events to end. He would order each musician of the orchestra to leave and turn off the lights until the guests left.

Alexander was afraid of horses. In his childhood, he had had an unpleasant experience on a bad-tempered mount. His wife once convinced him to go on a carriage ride with her. As he reluctantly entered the carriage, the ponies reared back. He immediately left the carriage and no amount of pleading from his wife could convince him to get back in.

Raymond "Ray" Crane (born October 31, 1930, Skegness - died June 29, 1994) was a British jazz trumpeter. Crane played locally in his twenties and early thirties, then became a member of Bruce Turner's band in 1963, which significantly raised his profile. He later played in the ensembles of Brian Lemon and Stan Greig, and worked with touring American trumpeters such as Red Allen, Bill Coleman, and Ray Nance. He also worked as a musical pedagogue, teaching and leading a youth jazz band which graduated Martin Taylor and Guy Barker. References "Ray Crane". The New Grove Dictionary of Jazz. 2nd edition, ed. He also worked as a musical pedagogue, teaching and leading a youth jazz band which graduated Martin Taylor and Guy Barker.

Cochinitos de piloncillo, also known as marranitos, cochinitos and puerquitos (all meaning "little pigs" in Spanish), are a typical Mexican sweet bread (pan dulce) made with "piloncillo"—a type of sweetener made from sugar cane. Cochinitos are popular in bakeries in Mexico and throughout the US. Cochinitos de piloncillo are an oven-cooked pastry which forms a part of the Huastecan gastronomy in the northern section of the Gulf of Mexico in Mexico. The type of bread these treats are made from is chichimbré, the name chichimbré is a deformation of gingerbread. Gingerbread 
was brought by the English to Mexico during and after the First World War for the extraction of oil in Mexico, today ginger is no longer added, but instead other spices such as cinnamon and anise

Susan Braudy (born Susan Orr July 8, 1941) is an American author and journalist.

Early life and education
Braudy grew up in Philadelphia and relocated to Manhattan, New York. She received her undergraduate degree from Bryn Mawr College and attended University of Pennsylvania and Yale University graduate schools, where she studied ethics and aesthetics.

Braudy's father Bernard Orr worked for the Philadelphia Housing Authority and actively supported local artists such as Dox Thrash. He was Vice President of the American Jewish Committee and his Master's thesis at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania became the book Technological Unemployment, an early look at how advances in technology were replacing human labor. He was the principal of a vocational night school whose students were largely African-American. Braudy's mother Blanche Orr taught history at Germantown High School, whose students were also largely African-American, and went back to school to become a reading supervisor because her students needed better reading skills. Braudy now lives with film editor Joe Weintraub.

Career
Braudy has written for The New York Times, Newsweek, The Atlantic Monthly, The Huffington Post, Harper's Magazine, Glamour, Vanity Fair, Ms., New York Magazine, The New Journal, Jezebel and The Week. She was the first woman writer hired by Newsweek.

Braudy had been commissioned by Playboy magazine in 1969 to write an "objective" piece on the feminism movement. Her final article was viewed as controversial by male Playboy editors. The debate continued up to Hugh Hefner; who wrote in a memo (covertly distributed by female Playboy employees) that he felt the article needed to focus more on the "highly irrational, emotional, kookie trend" of feminism because "these chicks [are] the natural enemy of Playboy." He argued that radical feminists were rejecting the Playboy way of life. Braudy later wrote an article published in Defiance and Glamour magazine in which she analyzed the contents of Hefner's memo and criticized his approach to women.

Braudy was an editor and writer at Ms. magazine. She edited the October 1975 men's issue of Ms. whose cover featured Robert Redford's back.

In 1977, Braudy became an associate of the Women's Institute for Freedom of the Press (WIFP). WIFP is an American nonprofit publishing organization. The organization works to increase communication between women and connect the public with forms of women-based media.

In 1981, Braudy was appointed Vice President of East Coast Production at Warner Brothers. She worked as Vice President of Michael Douglas's Stonebridge Production Company from 1986 to 1989. She was hired by Francis Ford Coppola, Jerry Bruckheimer, Martin Scorsese, and Oliver Stone to write screenplays.

Her article on paperback auctions, published in The New York Times magazine, was used by the Federal Trade Commission for an anti-trust suit against the high-bidder in a multimillion-dollar paperback rights auction.

In 2006 Braudy judged the Lukas Prize, the award from the Columbia University Journalism School and the Nieman Foundation for Journalism at Harvard, given annually to recognize excellence in book-length investigative journalism.

Accusations against Michael Douglas
On January 18, 2018, Braudy accused former colleague Michael Douglas of sexual harassment in an article for The Hollywood Reporter. She contended that during her time at Stonebridge Productions, she was "subjected to sexual harassment by Douglas that included near-constant profane and sexually charged dialogue, demeaning comments about her appearance, graphic discussions regarding his mistresses," and finally masturbating in front of her.

Afonso II (; English: Alphonzo; Archaic Portuguese: Affonso; Portuguese-Galician: Alfonso or Alphonso; Latin: Alphonsus; 23 April 118525 March 1223), nicknamed the Fat (o Gordo) or the Leper (o Gafo), was the third king of Portugal and the second but eldest surviving son of Sancho I of Portugal and Dulce of Aragon. Afonso succeeded his father on 27 March 1211. Reign As a king, Afonso II set a different approach of government. Hitherto, his father Sancho I and his grandfather Afonso I were mostly concerned with military issues either against the neighbouring Kingdom of Castile or against the Moorish lands in the south. Afonso did not pursue territory enlargement policies and managed to ensure peace with Castile during his reign. Despite this, some towns were conquered from the Moors by the private initiative of noblemen and clergy, as when Bishop Soeiro Viegas initiated the conquest of Alcácer do Sal. This does not mean that he was a weak or somehow cowardly man. The first years of his reign were marked instead by internal disturbances between Afonso and his brothers and sisters. The king managed to keep security within Portuguese borders only by outlawing and exiling his kin. Since military issues were not a government priority, Afonso established the state's administration and centralized power on himself. He designed the first set of Portuguese written laws. These were mainly concerned with private property, civil justice, and minting. Afonso also sent ambassadors to European kingdoms outside the Iberian Peninsula and began amicable commercial relations with most of them.

Other reforms included the always delicate matters with the pope. In order to get the independence of Portugal recognized by Rome, his grandfather, Afonso I, had to legislate an enormous number of privileges to the Church. These eventually created a state within the state. With Portugal's position as a country firmly established, Afonso II endeavoured to weaken the power of the clergy and to apply a portion of the enormous revenues of the Catholic Church to purposes of national utility. These actions led to a serious diplomatic conflict between 
the pope and Portugal. After being excommunicated for his audacities by Pope Honorius III, Afonso II promised to make amends to the church, but he died in Coimbra on 25 March 1223 before making any serious attempts to do so. King Afonso was buried originally at the Monastery of Santa Cruz in Coimbra where his body remained for nearly ten years. His remains were transferred subsequently to Alcobaça Monastery, as he had stipulated in his will. He and his wife, Queen Urraca, were buried at its Royal Pantheon. Marriage and descendants In 1206, he married Urraca, daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile and Eleanor of England. The couple were both descendants of King Alfonso VI of León. The offspring of this marriage were: Sancho II (8 September 12074 January 1248), king of Portugal; Afonso III (5 May 121016 February 1279), king of Portugal;
Eleanor (1211–1231), queen of Denmark Ferdinand (1218–1246), lord of Serpa

Out of wedlock, he had two illegitimate sons:
João Afonso (d. 9 October 1234), buried in the Alcobaça monastery; Pedro Afonso (d. after 1249), who accompanied his brother King Afonso in the conquest of Faro in 1249. He had an illegitimate daughter named Constança Peres.

Ancestry

School-Based HPV Vaccination Program, Shawnee County

Internal wiki page for the Community Health Nursing team. Maintained by program coordinator Lillian Achterberg, with contributions from the school nurse network in Topeka, Silver Lake and Auburn-Washburn districts.

Why This Program Exists

Kansas has one of the lower HPV vaccination completion rates in the region, and in Shawnee County only about 52 percent of adolescents aged thirteen to seventeen had completed the series as of the last state report. Many families simply miss the second dose, because it falls six to twelve months after the first and is rarely tied to a routine visit. Offering vaccination at school, with parental consent, removes the need for an extra appointment and has raised completion rates in similar Kansas counties by roughly fifteen points.

Program Calendar

We visit each participating middle school twice per academic year, once in October and once in April, so a student who starts the series in the fall can finish it in the spring. The district calendar on the shared drive lists confirmed dates, the assigned nurse, and the gym or classroom to be used. Please do not change a date directly in the calendar; send requests to Lillian so she can coordinate with the principal.

Consent Handling

Paper consent forms go home in the first week of September, and an electronic version is available through the district parent portal. Only signed consent from a parent or legal guardian is acceptable. Nurses should verify on the day that:
• The consent form is signed and dated within the current school year.
• The student's name and birth date match the class roster.
• The state immunization registry shows no dose given in the past five months.
• Any allergy or prior reaction noted on the form has been reviewed by the supervising nurse.

Talking With Families

Some parents have questions about why the vaccine is offered at eleven or twelve rather than later. The short answer is that the immune response is stronger at younger ages, which is why only two doses are needed before the fifteenth birthday instead of three. Nurses should share the CDC fact sheet, answer questions honestly, and never pressure a family. A respectful conversation that ends without consent is still a good outcome, and many families sign up the following semester.

Reporting

Enter every dose in the registry the same day, and complete the clinic tally sheet before leaving the building. Monthly totals feed into the report Lillian sends to the county health officer, Dr. Samuel Okafor.

Ningaloo Reef Monitoring Program: quarterly partners meeting

Exmouth Shire Council chambers and online, 4 September 2026, 9.30 am to 12.15 pm

Chair: Dr Fiona Kettering, Australian Institute of Marine Science. Recorder: Callum Brierley, Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA).

Attendance

In the room were Fiona Kettering (AIMS), Callum Brierley and Jodie Mallard (DBCA Exmouth district), Ross Pittaway (Ningaloo Turtle Program), and Tanya Rigby (Exmouth Dive and Whalesharks). Joining online were Dr Hemi Wallace from the University of Western Australia and Shannon Eades representing the Nyinggulu Baiyungu traditional owners.

Item 1: Bleaching Update

Fiona presented results from the March and April surveys. Water temperatures off Coral Bay peaked at 30.1 degrees in late February, about 1.4 degrees above the long-term summer average. Moderate bleaching was recorded at 18 of 42 survey sites, mostly in shallow lagoon areas. Follow-up surveys in July found that roughly two thirds of bleached colonies had recovered their colour, though mortality was higher among branching Acropora than among massive Porites colonies.

Hemi noted that these results are better than the 2011 marine heatwave, when large areas of the southern reef experienced severe bleaching. He cautioned against reading too much into one season's recovery.

Item 2: Tourism Pressure

Tanya raised concern about anchor damage at Bundegi and Oyster Stacks, where visitor numbers have increased sharply since the new Exmouth marina expansion. Callum confirmed DBCA has received three complaints this year. Shannon said traditional owners want to be involved in any decision about new moorings, since some sites carry cultural significance.

Item 3: Data Sharing

The group discussed creating a shared online dashboard for reef condition data, which currently sits in separate spreadsheets at AIMS, DBCA and UWA. Everyone supported the idea in principle, but Hemi raised concerns about publishing site-level data that could direct visitors to vulnerable areas.

Agreed Actions

* Fiona to circulate the full bleaching report by 18 September
* Callum and Tanya to identify locations for six new public moorings and share with traditional owners for comment
* Hemi to draft a data-sharing agreement covering what information is published and at what resolution
* Shannon to arrange a site visit with DBCA rangers and elders to Oyster Stacks before the end of October
* Ross to report on turtle nesting numbers at the next meeting

Item 4: Funding

Fiona confirmed the program's AIMS funding is secure until June 2028. DBCA expects confirmation of state funding for additional ranger positions in the November budget review.

Next meeting: early December, date to be confirmed by email.

Guillaume de l'Aubespine de Châteauneuf (1547–1629) was a French diplomat in London between 1585 and 1589, involved in the affairs of Mary, Queen of Scots. He became the Marquis of Châteauneuf.

Family background
He was a son of Claude de l'Aubespine, baron de Châteauneuf and Jeanne Bochetel, a daughter of the diplomat Guillaume Bochetel. Her brother Jacques Bochetel de la Forest, had been a diplomat in London in the 1560s.

London and Mary, Queen of Scots
Châteauneuf succeeded Michel de Castelnau as ambassador in London in September 1585. He inherited packets of unsent ciphered letters for Mary. In February 1586, Châteauneuf complained to Francis Walsingham that his lodgings were small and had a bad smell, and made his daughter unwell. His wife was pregnant. He hoped that Walsingham would move him to an empty house belonging to Mary Sidney, Countess of Pembroke.

Walsingham had kept spies in Castelnau's household and now determined to intercept Mary's correspondence arriving at the French embassy. Walsingham's agent was the courier Gilbert Gifford. Châteauneuf later described how Gifford would carry secret letters from London to Mary at Chartley Castle. The letters were taken to the nearby houses of Catholic sympathisers, and then hidden in beer barrels for delivery. Her letters to London were delivered by couriers disguised as locksmiths, upholsterers, or other craftsmen.

Invisible ink and cipher codes
In March 1586, Mary wrote from Chartley to Châteauneuf about maintaining a secret correspondence. She suggested writing sometimes on supplies of white taffeta or fine linen using invisible ink made with alum. He also could write between the lines on certain pages of new books delivered to her secretary Claude Nau. Because she often received new slippers, it would be convenient for him to hide secret messages in the cork soles and heels. He should be sure that the slippers with secret letters should be discretely marked on the sole with a fingernail. A cipher alphabet key for their correspondence survives in the National Archives.

Babington Plot
Anthony Babington was captured in London and the event became a celebration with bonfires and the ringing of church bells. Some of Châteauneuf's servants were arrested during the search for Babington. It was said that the plan was to have Elizabeth shot on 15 August. Châteauneuf and another diplomat, Charles de Prunelé, Baron d'Esneval, who had recently returned from Scotland, had an audience with Elizabeth I at Windsor Castle, and Elizabeth declared that Mary, Queen of Scots, was behind the plot. In September 1586, Châteauneuf wrote to Courcelles, a French diplomat in Scotland, describing the arrest of Mary's secretaries Claude Nau and Gilbert Curle. Papers were seized which were used to implicate Mary in the Babington Plot.

Châteauneuf and his secretary Destrappes were thought be personally involved in the Babington Plot, or another plan to poison Elizabeth I, and he was questioned by William Cecil with the informer William Stafford, a brother of the ambassador in Paris, Edward Stafford. His answers were doubtful, and although it was thought Elizabeth requested his removal he remained in post. Châteauneuf discussed the release of Destrappes with Elizabeth at Croydon Palace in May.

Châteauneuf wrote a description of the discovery of the Babington Plot for Henry III of France. He worked in vain with a special envoy Pomponne de Bellièvre to argue against her execution. Guillaume de l'Aubespine de Châteauneuf (1547–1629) was a French diplomat in London between 1585 and 1589, involved in the affairs of Mary, Queen of Scots. He became the Marquis of Châteauneuf.

Family background
He was a son of Claude de l'Aubespine, baron de Châteauneuf and Jeanne Bochetel, a daughter of the diplomat Guillaume Bochetel. Her brother Jacques Bochetel de la Forest, had been a diplomat in London in the 1560s.

London and Mary, Queen of Scots
Châteauneuf succeeded Michel de Castelnau as ambassador in London in September 1585. He inherited packets of unsent ciphered letters for Mary. In February 1586, Châteauneuf complained to Francis Walsingham that his lodgings were small and had a bad smell, and made his daughter unwell. His wife was pregnant. He hoped that Walsingham would move him to an empty house belonging to Mary Sidney, Countess of Pembroke.

Walsingham had kept spies in Castelnau's household and now determined to intercept Mary's correspondence arriving at the French embassy. Walsingham's agent was the courier Gilbert Gifford. Châteauneuf later described how Gifford would carry secret letters from London to Mary at Chartley Castle. The letters were taken to the nearby houses of Catholic sympathisers, and then hidden in beer barrels for delivery. Her letters to London were delivered by couriers disguised as locksmiths, upholsterers, or other craftsmen.

Invisible ink and cipher codes
In March 1586, Mary wrote from Chartley to Châteauneuf about maintaining a secret correspondence. She suggested writing sometimes on supplies of white taffeta or fine linen using invisible ink made with alum. He also could write between the lines on certain pages of new books delivered to her secretary Claude Nau. Because she often received new slippers, it would be convenient for him to hide secret messages in the cork soles and heels. He should be sure that the slippers with secret letters should be discretely marked on the sole with a fingernail. A cipher alphabet key for their correspondence survives in the National Archives.

Babington Plot
Anthony Babington was captured in London and the event became a celebration with bonfires and the ringing of church bells. Some of Châteauneuf's servants were arrested during the search for Babington. It was said that the plan was to have Elizabeth shot on 15 August. Châteauneuf and another diplomat, Charles de Prunelé, Baron d'Esneval, who had recently returned from Scotland, had an audience with Elizabeth I at Windsor Castle, and Elizabeth declared that Mary, Queen of Scots, was behind the plot. In September 1586, Châteauneuf wrote to Courcelles, a French diplomat in Scotland, describing the arrest of Mary's secretaries Claude Nau and Gilbert Curle. Papers were seized which were used to implicate Mary in the Babington Plot.

Châteauneuf and his secretary Destrappes were thought be personally involved in the Babington Plot, or another plan to poison Elizabeth I, and he was questioned by William Cecil with the informer William Stafford, a brother of the ambassador in Paris, Edward Stafford. His answers were doubtful, and although it was thought Elizabeth requested his removal he remained in post. Châteauneuf discussed the release of Destrappes with Elizabeth at Croydon Palace in May.

Legal Summary: Liability of a Dive Operator for Anchor Damage to Coral in the Bonaire National Marine Park

Prepared by Mr. Ruben Hoekman, attorney at law in Kralendijk, for the Bonaire National Parks Foundation (STINAPA). The summary covers the judgment of the Court of First Instance of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba of 11 March 2026.

Facts

On 14 August 2025, a dive charter vessel operated by Blue Horizon Diving B.V. dropped anchor at the dive site known as Something Special, close to the harbour of Kralendijk. The vessel's captain, Mr Wim Jaspers, stated that he anchored because all public mooring buoys at the site were occupied and he wished to drop off divers quickly. The anchor and chain dragged across an area of reef estimated at 38 square metres, breaking several colonies of star coral and brain coral, some of which were estimated to be more than a century old. A ranger of the foundation documented the damage the same afternoon.

The Bonaire Marine Environment Ordinance prohibits anchoring within the marine park, which covers the entire coastline of the island from the high water line to a depth of 60 metres. The foundation claimed compensation for the cost of restoration and for the ecological loss.

Questions Addressed by the Court

The court considered the following issues:

• Whether the operator, as well as the captain, could be held liable for the breach of the anchoring ban
• Whether the unavailability of mooring buoys constituted a justification for anchoring
• How the ecological damage to the reef should be valued
• Whether the foundation could claim compensation for damage to a reef it does not own

Reasoning

The court held that the operator was liable for acts of its captain committed in the course of his duties, under the rules on employer liability in the Civil Code of the BES islands. It rejected the justification based on occupied buoys, noting that the captain could have waited or moved to another site, and that the anchoring ban admits no exceptions for commercial convenience.

On valuation, the court accepted a report by the foundation's marine scientist, Dr Lieke Dekker, which estimated the cost of stabilising broken colonies and transplanting nursery-grown coral at 46,000 US dollars. It declined, however, to award an additional sum for loss of ecological value, finding that the foundation had not provided a method for quantifying such loss with sufficient reliability.

On standing, the court held that the foundation, as the statutory manager of the marine park, was entitled to claim the costs it reasonably incurs in restoring damage, even though the seabed is public property.

Outcome and Significance

Blue Horizon Diving was ordered to pay 46,000 US dollars plus legal costs. The judgment confirms that dive operators bear responsibility for their crews and that restoration costs are recoverable. The foundation may wish to commission a methodology for valuing ecological loss so that future claims can include that element.
